subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO BENEFITS TO MEMBERS OF REGULAR FORCE SERVING IN KOREA

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO BENEFITS TO MEMBERS OF REGULAR FORCE SERVING IN KOREA
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief statement concerning veterans benefits for members of the regular forces who served in Korea. As hon. members know, Canadian servicemen fighting in Korea included not only career men from the regular forces but also men who had enlisted especially for the purpose of taking part in this operation. Those who had so enlisted especially for service in Korea, like their predecessors who had enlisted during the second world war, interrupted their civilian life to do their part in the defence of Canada and the free world. It was only proper, therefore, that while they were serving in the armed forces they should receive benefits similar to those given to the men serving during the second world war, and that when they ceased to be in the armed forces they should become entitled to the benefits of the veterans charter, under the Veterans Benefit Act.
As the regular forces expanded, however, the balance between the men who were especially enlisted for service in Korea and those who were career soldiers changed. Today, I am told, all but one of the young men who enlisted especially for service in Korea have been discharged or they have joined the regular forces. When hostilities ended it was considered appropriate to review the
eligibility for benefits of all Korean veterans, and it was felt that members of the regular forces who had served in the theatre of operations, and had been subjected to the same hardships and risks as their special force comrades, should be eligible for the same benefits.
Accordingly an order in council was passed on November 19, 1953, under the provisions of the Veterans Benefit Act, which makes such members of the regular forces eligible, upon discharge, for the same benefits as members of the special force.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
On
Friday evening, Mr. Speaker, I began to defend Senator McCarthy against the attack of the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), made in the house on November 23, 1953.
Before I proceed, may I just clarify my own position? I participate in this debate on my personal volition, and not in any way as a spokesman for the Social Credit group.
I now proceed with my defence of Senator McCarthy. May I give a measure of attention to Senator McCarthy himself? First, who is Senator McCarthy? Senator Joseph McCarthy is the head of the Senate investigations subcommittee. This can be verified from a Washington dispatch in the Ottawa Citizen of July 21, 1953. It must be quite obvious, consequently, to anyone who has a sense of reality that the senator is not likely to become a dictator or an American Hitler or anything nonsensical like that. He is not likely to become a graver menace than communism or any of the other "isms". All that type of propaganda is pure propaganda and is malicious, malignant and utterly unjustified.
Now, what set off Senator McCarthy on his determined course in hunting out subversive figures in the United States administration? It is an interesting story. When the senator first came as a freshman to Washington in December, 1946, he was greatly flattered upon receiving an invitation from, the secretary of the navy, James Forrestal, to lunch with Mr. Forrestal. Mr. Forrestal gave him a great deal of inside information which helped the young man to realize what it was, or apparently was, that seemed to be defeating the United States at every turn. He thanks God to this very day for that interview with that great figure.
Now secretary of state Byrnes in 1946 wrote a letter to Congressman Adolph Sabath telling that congressman that President Truman's own security officers had declared that there were 284 individuals employed in the State Department who ought to be dismissed for communist connections or sympathies. That rather puts a different light on the whole story, does it not?
Only 79 of those 284 were discharged. Therefore 205 individuals were still in the state department, on its payroll, even though President Truman's own personal security committee had recommended to him that those people be dismissed, and had declared them unfit for government service.
fMr. Diefenbaker.]

Now I will ask any man, any member in this House of Commons-and members in the House of Commons are of very high quality and responsibility-if they had been in a position similar to that of Senator McCarthy and had been given information like that, would they have laid down on the job? Would they have betrayed the responsibility and trust which was reposed in them? I seriously doubt it.
McCarthy, by whatever means he could possibly devise, was able to get the names of only 81 of those 205. McCarthy asked President Truman to have Dean Acheson give McCarthy the rest of the 205 names. Truman did not even answer McCarthy's telegram asking for them.
McCarthy asked the Tydings committee, before which he was called, to subpoena Acheson and get those 205 names. The Tydings committee did not do so, although presumably it was appointed to investigate the charges which McCarthy had made in a speech in the Senate.
President Truman issued a strict order on March 13, 1948, forbidding any government employee to give any congressional committee information concerning the loyalty of any person, or concerning the contents of any investigative files. Can you imagine that? Now, in the face of a situation like that, I think hon. members would realize that Senator McCarthy, to have got as far as he has got, must have done some remarkable work somewhere.
What seems to be the secret of his effectiveness? McCarthy assailed the top-notchers of the communist organization, the big fellows, the people whom most people cultivated- Acheson, Tydings, Jessup, Lattimore, Stevenson and Benton. All of them are now gone, but McCarthy still remains.
The little people all over the nation therefore liked and trusted him. It is easy enough to jump on the little, poor, weak fellow; but to jump on the big fellows requires courage and conviction.
McCarthy was and is a new and forceful figure with a new and vigorous voice, a dynamic personality with the ability to speak directly and to the point. He has the faculty of commanding public attention, and an insistent approach, a free-swinging style, and a remorseless attack. The communist organization assailed him immediately, with all the kinds of smear that it has at its disposal and that it uses against any man who begins to produce results against any of its people.

Senator McCarthy has proved that he has great courage and sincerity, great intellectual capacity tor learning facts and understanding world and national problems. He has displayed great pertinacity, great industry and great leadership. These facts, in the main, can be verified by consulting the introduction to Senator McCarthy's own book, "McCarthyism, The Fight For America", sent to the printer on May 18,	1952. This
introduction was written by William M. McGovern, professor of political science at Northwestern University in the United States.
Generally speaking, up to date what has been the net result of Senator McCarthy's efforts? As a result of his speeches, the man in the street, the average American citizen, became alerted to the perilous situation with which we are faced-and we are faced with a most perilous situation!
The one-time arrogant and bullying communist politburo, which only four short years ago nestled snugly and safely among American government officials, has been reduced to a rabble of trembling, pleading men, each reiterating anxiously that he has always been anti-communist.
No wonder communists and communist sympathizers are literally gnashing their teeth and screeching at Senator McCarthy! Communists will never forgive him for what he has done. He has let the cat out of the bag in every way; and unless they manage to assassinate him or otherwise effectively dispose of him he will let the rest of the cats out of the bag-and they are pretty ugly cats!
It might, with truthfulness, be said that McCarthy has taken much of the fight out of communism and pro-communism. In particular, Senator McCarthy has exposed the following members of that once bullying communist junta:	Owen Lattimore, John
Stewart Service, John Carter Vincent, William T. Stone, Esther Brunauer and Philip Jessup. Every one of those six public figures whom McCarthy has exposed protested absolute innocence when McCarthy named them. The final conclusion, however, was that McCarthy was right. They are gone.
Now, what are the common attacks levied against McCarthy? The first one is that he is often called too hard-boiled. Communists, Mr. Speaker, are exceedingly difficult and ugly customers to master. They have three main types of technique in their attempt to appeal to men's sympathies. They have beautiful and high-sounding talk about their Americanism and their absolute patriotism. They have unctuous idealism and zeal for human rights. Then, they employ twisted
The Address-Mr. Blackmore publicity-just take a look at the newspapers which will go out reporting this speech I am giving now and you will know the kind of publicity I mean. You will get the idea of who the communist sympathizers are. In addition to these, they resort to blackmail and plain goon violence. It is not easy to deal with them.
Again, Senator McCarthy is charged with unfeelingly involving innocent people in his investigations and attacks. The facts, Mr. Speaker, do not bear out this charge. To support this statement of mine, may I read from the American Mercury of September, 1953. This is a passage which I think must be accepted until some hon. member is prepared to refute it. This article is headed "The Truth About Joe McCarthy", and states, in part:
So painstakingly careful is McCarthy to avoid reputation-damaging publicity for the individual who may be innocent, that he follows a strict rule of private, unpublicized examinations at which the accused is given full opportunity to clear himself.
Sometimes these examinations are repeated several times. Only after the evidence of communism or pro-communism is overwhelming is the subject subpoenaed for a full-dress, publicized open hearing. This punctilious regard for fair play guides all the McCarthy inquiries.
The truth of this may be found in the way in which he dealt with Owen Lattimore, one of the most difficult men he had to deal with.
In a similar way we can show that all the other charges that are laid against Joe McCarthy are simply unfounded. They are manufactured for the sole purpose of blackening this man, discrediting him in the eyes of the people, so that the people of the United States and of the world will not learn the remarkable things which his industry and persistence have divulged, so as to warn them.
May I once more quote the definition Truman gave of McCarthyism as it was put on the record by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) at page 237 of Hansard. I quote first the words of the hon. member:
I am prepared to accept the definition given by a former president of the United States who has lived in a close and intimate fashion with McCarthyism. Here is his definition, as reported in the Globe and Mail of November 17:
"It is a corruption of truth, the abandonment of our historical devotion to fair play.
"It is the abandonment of the due process of law.
"It is the use of the big lie and the unfounded accusation against any citizen in the name of Americanism or security.
"It is the rise to power of the demagogue who lives on untruth.
"It is the spread of fear and the destruction of faith in every level of our society."
Joe McCarthy is just exactly the opposite to that, Mr. Speaker. This fact can be

The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe established by documentation beyond any possibility of question. I have the means right here on my desk. Every charge in the Truman statement, which I have already quoted, is altogether false, if it was meant to apply to Senator Joseph McCarthy. These charges which Truman makes are true concerning the communist organization of the United States. There is no depth of human depravity to which these communist people will not resort in their attempts to undermine and destroy those who have incurred their displeasure by establishing the truth.
I think I will close these remarks at this time, Mr. Speaker. I do not wish to burden the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the end of the war, I have usually taken advantage of the opportunity afforded by this debate to comment on the state of the Canadian economy.
In general, I think it is fair to say that my annual remarks about economic conditions and prospects in Canada have been a good deal more optimistic than the remarks made by members of the opposition parties. Indeed, my steady confidence has usually been in marked contrast with the gloomy predictions of some opposition speakers who have been quite sure that under the present government, the country was going to the dogs.
Looking back at what has actually happened in Canada since I began making these annual reviews, it is evident not only that the gloomy prophets were talking through their hats1, but that I was far from overoptimistic in what I had to say. In the light of events, in the light of the high level of prosperity and the high rate of growth and development which has prevailed in post-war years, I did in fact consistently underestimate the strength of the Canadian economy.
I suppose the opposition feel they have to take a gloomy view, that it would be bad

politics to admit that the country is prospering under a Liberal administration. It might almost be said that the opposition have a vested interest in depression. As for me, I shall continue to have faith in Canada and I shall continue to advocate and support the policies that have raised this country to its present enviable position among the nations of the world.
I have faith in the future of Canada. But I am not one of those, if indeed there are any such, who believe that in a free economy every industry, in every part of the country, can expect to be profitable and fully employed at all times. Least of all do I think that in a country like Canada, dependent as it is to such a high degree on external trade, it is reasonable to expect that everything that people would like to produce will always be saleable at the prices the producers would like to obtain. The world is not being run solely to suit Canadians.
What strikes me as most significant about the present situation is that here in Canada, and I think in every other country where there is reasonable freedom, conditions are becoming more competitive. The period of post-war inflation, which was given a shot in the arm by Korea, seems to have come to an end. The sellers' market has to all intents and purposes disappeared. The buyer is in a stronger bargaining position than he has been for many years.
This is a healthy development, far healthier indeed than the indefinite continuation of a situation in which costs and prices are being pushed up by the pressure of excess demand. Inflation breeds slump and the sooner inflation can be brought to a halt, the smaller the resulting distortion.
Fortunately for all of us, now and in the future, inflationary tendencies were never permitted to get out of hand in Canada. There has, of course, been a substantial rise in general price levels since the end of the war but most of this was unavoidable, the inevitable consequence of world-wide forces. As a result of our internal fiscal, monetary and credit policies and related measures, coupled with our multilateral trading policies, Canada experienced as little inflation as any country and a good' deal less than most.
For that reason the adjustment to a more competitive situation has not caused, and should not cause, serious difficulties for the Canadian economy as a whole, although it may for particular industries and particular firms. I think it can be said that we have been building on pretty solid foundations.
Evidence that this is so is to be found in the continued high level of Canadian economic

activity. 1953 has been an extraordinary year by any measure. Total output will exceed $24 billion, probably more than 5 per cent above 1952. Since price levels have been more or less stable over the past year, this represents an equivalent increase in real output in line with the increase achieved in each of the three preceding years.
As output rose, so did employment. Even with the steady rise in the labour force, augmented by large numbers of new immigrants, there has been very little increase in unemployment.
Up to mid-1952 much of the increase in production and employment could be traced to defence expenditure and to intensified world demand for strategic materials. Since that time, however, the main impetus has come from increased demand for goods and services to raise standards of living.
Of particular importance has been the rapidly growing appetite of the Canadian consumer. Total consumer purchases in physical volume terms are running about 12 per cent above the level of two years ago. This is much the sharpest rise that has taken place since 1946. It may interest hon. members to know that the increased flow of goods and services to Canadian consumers accounts for two-thirds of the addition to total national output during the past two years.
Sales of automobiles and household appliances have been remarkably buoyant. In part this reflects the substantial increase in instalment buying that began early in 1952. It should be noted, however, that the increase in consumer buying has been spread throughout all the main consumer goods, including soft as well as hard goods. Food consumption, for example, has risen by 12 per cent in two years.
Underlying this broad growth in consumer spending has been the strong upward trend of personal incomes, in real as well as in money terms. Prior to 1952, money incomes, although increasing substantially, did little more than keep pace with rising prices. By the beginning of 1952 consumer prices had levelled off and have since remained slightly below the peak reached in January, 1952. At the same time, average earnings continued to rise. The result has been a continuing and substantial improvement in real earnings of wage and salary earners, professional people and most other groups. It has been estimated, for example, that average weekly earnings of those working for wages and salaries has increased by 16 per cent during the past two years and the trend continues. As for farm incomes, lower prices for some farm products have to some extent offset the unusually
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe large grain crops harvested in recent years. Even so, 1953 farm incomes, though below the levels of 1951 and 1952, remain well above those of any earlier years.
Nor are consumers dipping into their savings to maintain this high rate of spending. Individuals, on the average, are still managing to save 8 or 9 cents of each dollar currently earned, a rate which, on the basis of past experience, may be considered as pretty high.
Consumer spending has been rising. And so has expenditure for the purpose of increasing Canadian capacity to produce. Indeed, I am frank to admit that the rate of capital formation has exceeded my fondest hopes. I would not have been at all surprised if capital expenditure had levelled off this year. But such has not been the case. 1952 established a new record. The latest estimates indicate that capital outlays this year may reach $5-6 billion, a figure 9 per cent greater than the previous record established in 1952. Since prices of capital goods have been more or less stable, this 9 per cent increase represents an equivalent increase in terms of plant and equipment put in place.
I am not going to attempt to predict the level of capital investment in 1954. My department is gathering information as to the intentions of businessmen and governments for next year which will not be available in sufficient detail for some weeks to come. But the limited evidence already in seems to point to a continuation of a high level of investment expenditure.
I have heard fears expressed about what would' happen when some of the huge resource development projects now under way are completed. Will there be a sudden and sharp drop in investment expenditures? I think not. On the contrary, I am inclined to believe that the investment in basic industrial capacity now going on is part of a fundamental expansion in the productive capacity of this country, which is far from completed and which still retains much of its impetus. Korea served to speed up the development of resources which would otherwise have taken place more gradually. This concentration of effort in turn brought forward the need for expansion of secondary and service facilities which are necessary for a full and rounded development of the country.
It follows that while the gradual completion of some of the large resource projects initiated since 1950 may well bring a change in the composition of total investment, there will not necessarily be a sharp reduction in

The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe total expenditure. In 1954 capital outlays in basic material industries may be lower. This decline could be offset by a further increase in utility, service and institutional investment.
Let me run quickly over some of the developments that are in prospect. In some industries like industrial chemicals, primary iron and steel and the processing of metals like copper and aluminum, the emphasis is shifting from the creation of new facilities to the modernization of existing plants. Much the same thing is happening in pulp and paper.
Assuming reasonable free access to the United States market, Canadian sales of aluminum are likely to be such as to necessitate completion of further stages of the Kiti-mat project.
Turning to the development of sources of energy, the outlook is most encouraging. A long-term coal modernization program is under way. Even more money than in 1953 may be spent on the development of new sources of hydro power, oil and natural gas.
As for natural gas, the imagination of the Canadian people has been stirred

and with reason-by the prospect that lies ahead. The authorization at all levels-provincial, federal and international-of one or more long distance gas pipe lines will do more than encourage the drilling for oil in Western Canada. It will attract hundreds of millions of dollars of new capital-capital to pay for gas treating and chemical plants, gas gathering and transmission lines, gas distributing systems and gas using equipment. All this will take time. But, as electricity did in the past, so natural gas promises to usher in yet another era in Canada's march to industrial maturity.
All told, hundreds of millions, and perhaps even billions of dollars, are involved in the further development of Canadian resources. Projects of this magnitude, on top of those which are already under way, will do much to maintain activity in the months and years ahead.
I am also very glad to be able to report that Canadians are building more dwellings than ever before in their history. Starts, including conversions, may reach, if not exceed, 100,000 housing units in 1953. Last year the total was 86,000 housing starts and the previous record was 95,000 in 1950. There are good reasons for believing that house building will continue at a high level in 1954.
Time will not permit me to discuss defence procurement at any great length on this occasion. Later on I look forward to speaking on this subject. During the past fiscal year, defence procurement has amounted to nearly 6 per cent of the gross national product, and the present level is likely to be maintained for

the immediate future. Four programs-aircraft, shipbuilding, electronics and construction-make up about three-quarters of the total activity in this field.
An important step has been the abolition of the remaining Canadian controls on the use of materials. The defence program is no longer causing undue pressure on supplies, since our economy is now well adjusted to present levels of defence procurement. So far in this review of the general economic position, I have dealt with what might be termed the main internal determinants of economic activity-consumer spending, capital expenditures and expenditures by the government for defence purposes. It remains to discuss what, in some respects, is the key factor-external trade, which has such a profound influence upon the incomes of Canadians and upon their investment plans.
When the government, at the beginning of 1953, made a survey for its own internal use of trade prospects, the conclusion was reached that there would probably be some decline in exports below the levels of 1952 and quite a considerable increase in imports. Some decline in exports seemed likely because of lower price levels for some of our stable products, and the more stringent import restrictions being imposed by dollar-short countries, and some increase in imports because of the high level of personal incomes, a world-wide improvement in the availability of goods of all kinds and the declared intentions of Canadian businessmen to proceed with a record program of capital expenditure.
On the whole, things have turned out pretty well as was expected. The surplus in our balance of payments on current account in 1952 has been converted into a deficit, without, I might add, any weakening in the Canadian dollar, which now stands at a premium of well over 2 per -cent. The fact that the exchange rate has remained strong is, I suggest, evidence that confidence in Canada has not been at all impaired by the change in the current account position from a surplus to a deficit. It is not unusual for a country in Canada's position-prosperous and building up its productive capacity at a rapid rate-to experience a moderate deficit on current account, financed by a net import of capital.
Exports during the first nine months of 1953 were about 3 per cent lower in value than in 1952 but when allowance is made for the lower -average prices being realized for Canadian exports, the actual volume of exports is very little, if any, short of the record established in 1952. Exports during

the months of May, June and July were in fact greater in both volume and value than the corresponding months of 1952.
The renewed efforts by dollar-short countries to achieve balance in dollar trade had the expected effects. As examples: Canadian exports to commonwealth countries during the first nine months of 1953 were 13 per cent below the same months of 1952; exports to Brazil, which is in the midst of an acute exchange crisis, fell by 50 per cent.
On the other hand, our exports were pretty well maintained or continued to rise to overseas countries in which Canadian goods were less subject to discriminatory restrictions, or which are largely dependent upon imports of food and basic raw materials. I refer to such countries as Germany and Japan which have become two of our best customers; Venezuela, one of the richest of the Latin American markets; the Netherlands, to which in the first nine months of this year we exported goods valued at $32 million compared with $26 million in the same period of 1952; and Belgium and Luxembourg, which ranks fifth among Canada's export markets.
In 1952 there was a shift in Canada's export trade towards overseas countries. This year there has been a shift in the opposite direction. During the first nine months of 1953 the United States took 59 per cent of our exports, as against 53 per cent in the same period of 1952. It is the policy 'of the government to sell Canadian goods throughout the free world. That is why we are always working towards the removal of trade restrictions. But if we cannot sell our goods in one place we must try to sell them in another. I am not concerned by the very substantial increase in exports to the United States. On the contrary, I have instructed my department and Canadian trade commissioners in the United States to do everything possible to promote sales of Canadian goods in that market.
There should never be any relaxation in the efforts of government and businessmen to build up export markets, even when prospects do not seem to be too good. Hon. members will recall that in the early part of this year I had the privilege of leading a Canadian good-will and trade mission composed of prominent Canadian businessmen and officials to nine countries in Latin America. We went because we realized that Latin America is a rich and developing area to which Canada was selling a very large volume of goods and to which we might be able to sell even more. It has not surprised me and I am sure it has not surprised 83276-29
The Address-Riaht Hon. C. D. Howe my business colleagues who went with me that some of these Latin American countries have had to reduce their purchases from dollar countries. That seemed to be in prospect even when we were there. This drop in exports to Latin America has not altered to the slightest degree my view that this is a rich and developing market which Canadian exporters should watch and cultivate.
While I am speaking about trade promotion it may interest the house to have a brief report on the Canadian international trade fair. Participation in the sixth fair held this June represented a 35 per cent increase in space over the largest of any of the previous fairs. It is most encouraging to find that participation by Canadian manufacturers and agents accounted for 145,200 square feet out of a total of 264,800 square feet. Attendance of business visitors from Canada showed an appreciable increase over the previous fair, while the attendance of businessmen from the United States was more than double the number who attended the fair in 1952.
Plans for the 1954 fair are already under way and the bookings for space to the end of October reached a total of 173,230 square feet. Out of this total, bookings by Canadian manufacturers and agents amounts to 96,000 square feet.
It is my opinion that this Canadian international trade fair is steadily increasing its usefulness in assisting my department in its work of promoting international trade.
The next several months may bring important developments in the field of international economic relations. Basic questions of policy are now being re-examined in the United States, in the United Kingdom and in other major trading countries. We are hopeful that the conclusions and decisions to be reached will make possible some real and effective progress towards the goals of convertibility of currencies and freer trade.
In the United States, an important commission has been appointed to study all aspects of foreign economic policy. I am sure that the purposes and objectives of the United States in the broad field of world trade are fundamentally akin to our own and that the constructive leadership that the United States has provided since the end of the war will be strengthened and re-affirmed. The decisions of the United States government in this matter are bound to be of crucial importance to the future of world trade. They will be of particularly vital and direct concern to Canada, as the United States' major and closest trading partner.
In the meantime, there have been encouraging signs that many other countries are
450	HOUSE OF
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe prepared in their own interests to move ahead as far as possible with policies that will bring freedom of trade and convertibility of currencies nearer. Hon. members are aware that the United Kingdom has instituted a policy of relaxing import restrictions on basic materials and foodstuffs and of moving towards a non-discriminatory basis of importing such commodities. I would hazard the opinion, shared I think by many in the United Kingdom, that this policy adopted in the dark days of a sterling crisis has contributed substantially to the improvement in the financial position of the U.K. The government of South Africa has very recently taken a step of great importance in wholly removing the discrimination in its import control system. Canadian exporters of manufactured goods have suffered from discrimination against them in commonwealth markets in recent years and I regard it as highly significant that they will now have an equal chance to compete for business in their traditional South African markets.
In Europe, the Netherlands recently announced removal of discrimination against dollar goods in a wide range of imports which had previously been subject to restriction. In other countries, we know that careful attention is being given to the advantages which ensue from the removal of discriminatory restrictions, particularly in the field of foodstuffs, basic raw materials, capital goods and machinery. I am optimistic, therefore, that further progress will be made in the freeing of trade during the coming year.
These are all signs pointing to the kind of trading world we have been striving and working for these last several years. I wish to express the Canadian government's gratification at the courageous and foresighted moves taken thus far by several countries in the face of many uncertainties. It is becoming increasingly clear to many countries that import restrictions in themselves are no solution to the exchange difficulties that have so hampered trade in the post-war world. Indeed, I think that a cause and effect relationship is being more and more recognized whereby freer imports of essential materials and foodstuffs, by reducing costs of production and internal price levels, enable countries to compete more effectively and thus to strengthen their exchange reserves.
Canada has been consistent in its approach to world trade problems, and I believe that recent experience has increasingly confirmed the validity of our approach. We have repeatedly expressed our views as to the desirability of relaxing trade barriers over the widest possible area. We have repeatedly stressed our belief that such action would


effectively contribute to the strength of the trading community as a whole, and to the improvement of exchange reserves in particular countries. We shall continue to play our full part in supporting all efforts directed towards convertibility and the promotion of high levels of multilateral trade.
I had the pleasure not long ago of leading the Canadian delegation to the eighth session of the contracting parties to the general agreement on tariffs and trade in Geneva. The GATT, by reducing trade barriers and by defining agreed rules of conduct in international trade, has been one of the main elements of stability in the world trade picture in recent years. I was personally impressed with the businesslike and cordial atmosphere that prevails in GATT meetings, and came away from Geneva fully convinced of the value of the general agreement as a central instrument for international trade relations. This was an important session, for a decision had to be reached as to the status of the tariff schedules negotiated by GATT countries on three separate occasions since 1947. On behalf of the Canadian government, I proposed a firm binding of these schedules for a further definite period, pending clarification of the trading policies of major countries. Other countries agreed with this approach as being in the common interest. I am happy to say that agreement has been reached to maintain for a further period of 18 months the important and extensive tariff gains achieved thus far under the GATT. This decision is indicative of a desire on the part of many countries to continue on a road that has proved its practical value and which holds real promise for the future. It is hoped that as the policies of major countries become more clearly defined, it may be possible next year to undertake a constructive re-examination of the general agreement as a whole, to adapt its basic provisions to the lessons and experiences of recent years and to the new plans and proposals that may emerge for the future. We in Canada will be particularly anxious to see a review of those provisions of the agreement that permit countries in balance-of-payments difficulties to apply restrictions and, in certain circumstances, to discriminate in such restrictions. We feel that more adequate consideration will now have to be given in the agreement to the kind of measures that will contribute effectively to the solution of exchange difficulties. In the light of such a review of the basic provisions of the agreement, and in the light also of the policy decisions to be reached by major trading countries, it may be found possible and

desirable to conduct further tariff negotiations. When that time comes, I am sure Canada will be ready and willing to play her full part.
Another important step taken by the contracting parties at the recent session of the GATT concerns Japan. Canada, together with a substantial majority of GATT countries, agreed to a formal decision inviting Japan to participate in the meetings and work of the contracting parties during a period when it is waiting to become a full party to the agreement. This does not in itself result in the application of the GATT as between GATT countries and Japan. However, the GATT countries also agreed at Geneva to a declaration whereby those countries able and willing to do so could enter into full GATT relations with Japan.
Canada has for some time been negotiating with Japan in the hope of finding an acceptable basis for a trade agreement between our two countries. The Canadian delegation in Geneva was instructed to state that, in the event of such an agreement being concluded, and subject to the terms of such an agreement, we would then be prepared to give serious consideration to having the GATT apply as between Canada and Japan.
Before concluding these rather discursive remarks it might be useful for me to attempt to draw the threads together and put Canada's general economic position and prospects before the house as I see them.
As I said at the outset, 1953 has been a remarkable year by any measure. Total output is at record levels. Price levels are more or less stable. Unemployment is very low. The country has been developing and expanding as never before. Export trade in physical terms is about as high as in the record year 1952. It has been a year of balanced prosperity.
And yet there have been problems, most of which are familiar to hon. members, and which I have no doubt they will bring to the government's attention, if they have not done so already.
The electric appliance industry has been experiencing some difficulty. Sales of electrical appliances have been unusually heavy for more than a year. Yet during 1953 both production and imports have been more than keeping pace with sales. As a result there are signs of an excessive accumulation of inventories in some appliance lines.
Another of the so-called soft spots is textiles. During 1953 to date economic activity in the textile industries is above the levels of the previous year even though many firms, particularly in the primary textile 83276-29i
The Address-Right Hon. C. D. Howe group, continue to operate below capacity. Retail clothing sales have been much better. At the same time imports of both clothing and primary textiles have been increasing and inventories of finished goods, particularly at retail, are higher than a year ago.
Another industry to encounter declining markets this year is the farm implements group. This situation has come about more as a result of the unusually high volume of sales in immediately preceding years than from any abnormally depressed market at the present time. As a result of bumper crops harvested in Canada and the United States in 1951 and 1952, sales of farm implements soared to record heights. While unusually good crops have again been harvested this year, equipment sales have moved in line with the moderate decline in over-all farm incomes. This downward trend has been accentuated by lower shipments to other foreign markets attributable largely to exchange difficulties.
This does not exhaust the list of industries which currently face problems of finding markets but it does illustrate the type of adjustment which cannot be avoided even in conditions of general prosperity. It is important to recognize, as I said at the outset, that we are now moving away from the sellers' market which has prevailed more or less for several years. This change does not, however, mean that there will necessarily be a decline in the general volume of business and employment. It does mean that many Canadian industries will experience more intensive competition, both domestically and internationally. There is no way of avoiding the marketing problems involved in this situation so long as we wish to enjoy the broader benefits to be derived from the free international exchange of goods.
Looking to the year ahead there seems to be little indication of any serious interruption in the generally prosperous conditions now prevailing. In the United States there have been numerous predictions of a moderate decline in activity in 1954. The basis for these expectations has been explained in terms of lower defence outlays, reduced capital spending, inventory liquidation, a decline in housing, softening in the automobile market and a number of other reasons. I do not propose to examine the significance of each of these factors. It is perhaps worthwhile, however, to emphasize one point which seems to apply not only to the United States but to other economies as well, and that is, that the period through which we have been passing seems to have very few of the characteristics normally ascribed to a pre-recession boom. By and large, speculative excesses have been absent since
452	HOUSE OF
The Address

Right Hon. C. D. Howe 1951. Commodity prices have been following a steady to slightly downward trend and business sentiment, seemingly influenced by oft-stated reminders of the dangers of a postdefence let-down, has remained on the cautious side. In such circumstances, there is little tendency for businesses to become over-extended and vulnerable.
The present situation would appear to be one in which adjustments could occur in one or in several sectors without any danger of these multiplying into a general collapse.
In these circumstances we might confidently expect that, whatever adjustments take place in the United States economy in the immediate future, they are not likely to lead to any serious curtailment in sales of Canada's major export items to that country. With respect to overseas markets, prospects for wheat sales are reasonably good even though increased world supply is likely to bring some reduction from the record export levels of the last two years. Sales of other commodities in overseas markets have undergone some adjustment during the past year and the present trade volume appears in over-all terms to be firmly based.
Sales prospects are probably firmer at home than in export markets. There is every reason to look forward to a continued high level of capital spending. Moreover, the prospective shift in the investment program toward housing and commercial and institutional building will mean increased employment for each dollar of expenditure. Total business inventories have increased during 1953 but not unduly, having regard to the rise in business volume and the extensive liquidation which occurred in many lines during 1952. Government expenditure for defence and other purposes should continue to act as a stabilizing influence. That being so, personal incomes and personal spendings, in aggregate, should be fairly well sustained.
To sum up, continuation of generally stable market conditions in the period ahead is indicated. It must be taken into account, of course, that capacities are expanding and larger outlets are necessary to absorb the increasing volume of production. With the emergence of increasingly competitive conditions on an international scale, marketing problems will be encountered in some industries.
To express my forecast for 1954 in a few words: There are going to be troubles in some industries but, as for the general level of economic activity, I predict the pessimists are going to be wrong again.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Since this is the first time I have risen to speak during this session, Mr. Speaker, may I take the opportunity, as many other members have done, of offering my congratulations to you upon taking over the chair. I am sure we are going to have a very happy parliament with you as the presiding officer. Should it become necessary at any time for you, in the heat of debate, to call an hon. member to order I know that the charm with which you will do that will make it a pleasure for the offender to comply.
Although the speech from the throne gave a warning that heavy expenditures for defence must continue, and pointed out the process of maintaining and if necessary building up our defences to deter aggression, the government did not see fit to enlarge upon this part of the speech from the throne until the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) spoke in the house last Thursday, exactly two weeks after the debate had started. This extraordinary delay, I must say, surprised me very much.

The words used in the speech from the throne to which I referred can be found at page 4 of Hansard for November 12, 1953, and are as follows:
Much remains to be done before there can be a permanent and durable peace in the world. My ministers therefore consider it would be unwise for the free nations to slacken our efforts to build up and maintain the necessary strength to deter aggression and they intend to continue to work to that end.
On Thursday the Minister of National Defence gave the house a comprehensive review of the services rendered by our armed forces during the last six months, both in Korea and in Europe, in their endeavours to assist the free nations to stop aggression. I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the minister for the comprehensive review which he gave, and to assure him that all Canada is proud of the contribution made by our armed forces. We are grateful for the sacrifices that they have made in these operations. It was also with profound regret that we heard the long list of casualties incurred in Korea. We on this side of the house join in extending our deepest sympathy to the friends and relatives of the men who have given their lives for freedom's cause.
We regret also that many men have returned with their earning power diminished as a result of wounds received or of the hardships that they endured. The country expects this government to deal generously with these men, and to see that when they return to this country they are provided with ample opportunities to fit into the civilian life of the community. In his remarks the minister did not explain why it had been considered necessary to withdraw certain of the rehabilitation benefits to the Korean veterans.
It was not very long ago that amendments were made to the Veterans Benefit Act, in which the service of the men in Korea was to be recognized. The definition of a theatre of war in the old act was changed so as to include Korea, in order that men serving there might receive the benefits under veterans benefit regulations.
The definition originally given of service in a theatre of war referred to service of a member of the Canadian forces from the time of departure from Canada, or continental United States, including Alaska, before July 27, 1953, to participate in military operations undertaken by the United Nations to restore peace in the republic of Korea. And then it gives one or two qualifications under which a man may return home.
But in the regulations passed on Thursday, September 24, of this year, an addition was
The Address-Mr. Pearkes made setting out the date of October 31, 1953. So that if October 31, 1953, was reached before the operations in Korea to undertake peace had been terminated, these benefits also would be terminated. Actually October 31 was reached before the operations had ceased, because there is no excuse for our troops being stationed in Korea now, unless it is to restore peace in the republic of Korea. They are fulfilling the role of occupational forces, and are ready to act at any time, should the very uncertain armistice develop again into a flare-up of hostilities. The troops are there in those circumstances, and are ready to carry out whatever tasks they may be called upon to do.
So it would seem that perhaps the withdrawal of these benefits might have been a little premature. I did think that the minister would have explained why it was necessary to withdraw those benefits before the operations in Korea had ceased.
It was however with satisfaction that we heard that, both in the actual theatre of war, and during their periods of training at home and abroad, the services had lived up to the best Canadian traditions.
The minister then turned to the all-important question of the defence of this country, and of the plans that we and the United States are making to protect the North American continent from surprise air attack. He referred to a statement in the white paper, "Canada's Defence Program, 1953-54", which was issued last spring, and in which attention is called to the fact that there has been a substantial increase in the emphasis on the defence of North America against air attack.
When General Eisenhower, President of the United States, delivered his address in this chamber on November 14, he also spoke of the need for Canada and the United States to devise a way to protect the North American continent from any surprise attack by air. After calling attention to that fact, he went on to say, as reported at page 27 of Hansard:
The basic threat of communist purpose still exists. Indeed the latest Soviet communication to the western world is truculent, if not arrogant, in tone. In any event our security plans must now take into account Soviet ability to employ atomic attack on North America as well as on countries, friendly to us, lying closer to the borders of the U.S.S.R. Their atomic stockpile will, of course, increase in size, and means of delivery will improve as time goes on.
And when he refers to "their atomic stockpile" he is referring to the stockpile of the U.S.S.R. And then he went on:
Each of our two nations seeks a secure home for realization of its destiny. Defence of our soil presents a challenge to both our peoples. It is a common task.
454	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Pearkes
In this respect it is also interesting to note that General Gruenther, supreme commander of the allied powers in Europe, said in his address to the Atlantic community conference at Copenhagen this summer-and I quote from the text of his address as set out in the publication Freedom and Union, October issue:
The Soviets have an air force of some 20,000 operational planes, a large proportion of which are jets. To meet that air threat our air forces must be increased, and their effectiveness must be such that they will be ready to fight on an instant's notice. It is not sufficient to depend upon reserve air forces, for the reason that air attacks can develop with such devastating swiftness that we would not be able to mobilize air reserves in time.
If the basic threat of communist purpose still exists, as General Eisenhower suggests- and who can doubt his word-and if at any time they should attempt to achieve their purpose by force, the Soviets, having the initiative, could select the point of attack. Geographically speaking, the Soviets occupy a central or interior position. The free countries are an extended perimeter, stretching from western Europe, through the Mediterranean, across North Africa and out to the Far East and the North American continent.
Frequently the Soviets refer to that as encirclement. One can obtain the full impression of the extent of this perimeter, and the central position occupied by Russia, only by looking at a globe rather than a map. Therefore the Russians, should they decide to use force, will be able to strike anywhere on that extended perimeter. We do not know at what point they may strike. It is one of those difficulties inherent in all operations conducted on what used to be referred to as exterior lines.
It does not follow that the enemy will do so. Yet the fact is now established that he could, should he so decide, commence a war with a major air offensive against the North American continent, supported by a large air force carrying atomic weapons both for strategic and for tactical use, because the atomic weapon has now passed from the purely strategic into the tactical sphere of operations as well.
It is well that this possibility is now recognized, because heretofore any suggestion made from this side of the house, that an attack was a possibility which had to be considered, was always brushed aside, and we were told that only diversionary raids had to be considered.
Now, as to this air threat of some 20,000 operational planes, I am not stating that they are all going to be used against this continent; they could not all be used, but we do not know what proportion of 20,000 might be


used. Twenty thousand is the force we know the Russians have. We have a Canadian-United States network of radar stations to provide early warning, and such communication facilities as may exist to direct our fighter squadrons, Canadian and United States of America, against the attacker.
In his remarks last Thursday the minister dispelled the myth, which had been created, of an Arctic radar chain, claiming that the project had never reached the stage of discussion between governments. It is well that the minister did make this declaration, because, through press releases and from other sources, the impression has been created in the public mind that a radar chain did exist across the far north. A radar screen has been referred to at times. The minister referred to a radar screen on more than one occasion. In its place a modified system has been built up to give protection to the most vulnerable areas against the most likely forms of attack.
The minister referred to a system working upwards and outwards from the most likely targets. I must say that "upwards and outwards" rather reminds me of a certain revivalist hymn, but it may give an impression of the present radar screen.
Now, this system, together with its attendant communication system, is partly in operation, according to the minister's statement; but it is now clear that no national screen exists.
Of course, the fighter squadrons are the backbone of your defence; but then we were told in the white paper of 1953-54:
The first regular squadron, equipped with CF-100 all-weather, twin-engined, jet fighters, was recently formed and by the end of the fiscal year a number of these squadrons will be operating.
The minister did not say how many of these regular squadrons were operating, but I have seen statements referring to three squadrons being more or less in formation at the present time. The statement goes on:
Meanwhile, a number of squadrons of F-86E Sabres, destined as part of Canada's NATO air contribution have been in Canada available for the defence of this continent. As the last of these are sent to Europe during the year,-
Mind you, they have all gone now.
-their places will be taken by squadrons of CF-lOO's. Reserve squadrons now equipped with Vampires and Mustangs will be re-equipped with CF-100's as these become available.
At that time we were told that there were some twelve auxiliary fighter squadrons in Canada, so that gives us a picture of the Canadian air fighter squadrons which are available to meet the threat.

We do not know very much about the United States squadrons, but as far as I know, no United States squadrons have been equipped with that particular type of aircraft, the CF-100, which is considered so important for the air defence of this country.
I am not pressing at the moment for information regarding the number of fighter squadrons, either regular or auxiliary, which are available at the present time, but I do want to call attention to the remark contained in General Gruenther's address at Copenhagen in which he is still talking about the threat of the Soviet air force. This is what he said:
It is not sufficient to depend upon reserve air forces, for the reason that air attacks can develop with such devastating swiftness that we would not be able to mobilize air reserves in time.
Those members of parliament or others who have seen the CF-100 manoeuvring may well question the ability, both physical and' technical, of a part-time pilot or radio navigator, or ground crews, to handle these tremendously complicated machines that travel faster than sound, and can perform amazing acrobatics.
Unless supplied with a high percentage of regular personnel, we should exercise caution as to the degree of reliance to be placed on reserve fighter squadrons. Today the general complaint with the reserve fighter squadrons, who are not of course equipped with CF-lOO's but are equipped with Vampires and Mustangs, is that they do not have sufficient active personnel in their squadrons to enable them to fulfil their given role.
While I have for a number of years past advanced the theory that first priority should be given to the development of our air forces-and I still adhere to that principle- yet I recognize the fact that a well-balanced team of all three services is essential. The time has not yet come when war can be won solely by air power.
The Soviets, again according to General Gruenther:
. . . have a very large active land force in being consisting of 175 Soviet divisions, and approximately 70 satellite divisions.
And according to General Gruenther the Soviet divisions are for the most part well trained. He says:
The satellite divisions are less effective, but their effectiveness is steadily increasing.
The west cannot of course match division for division, because to maintain in being forces of that magnitude would place an intolerable strain upon our national economy and upon the national economy of the free nations. That is why General Gruenther
The Address-Mr. Pearkes and General Eisenhower have both placed such dependence on the reserve divisions.
Again quoting from General Gruenther's Copenhagen speech:
But those divisions must be good if they are to be employed against Soviet forces. The creation of adequate reserve forces means that a large proportion of NATO manpower will have to devote a considerable time each year to reserve training. That is inconvenient for the individuals concerned, and of course it tends to create economic strains.
I do not believe that the small number of our reserve army that trained in camp this year caused any great economic strain to Canada. I was surprised that the minister did not tell us what steps are being taken to meet our obligation in so far as the maintenance of reserves is concerned, which may some time have to be used with our NATO contribution. For years it has been the traditional policy of Canada to regard the non-permanent militia, as it used to be called, or what is now called the reserve army as the backbone of our land forces. Unfortunately of late very little attention has been paid to our reserve army. An announcement was made during the summer that a committee had been set up to consider the reorganization of this force along certain lines. In view of the importance attached to the reserve formation by the SHAPE commanders, I am surprised that the minister made no reference to plans for the reorganization of the reserve army. I hope he will take advantage of an early opportunity to bring the house up to date in that respect.
The warning sounded in the throne speech and echoed by President Eisenhower here a few days later indicates that heavy expenditures will continue. President Eisenhower said:
The threat is present . . . now is the time for action on all agreed measures.
I thought the minister dealt with this statement very cautiously on Thursday. He said, as reported on page 365 of Hansard:
-there is complete agreement on the vital importance of effective methods of joint defence against direct attack.
The assurance that action was now being taken on all agreed measures was lacking. The minister used somewhat uncertain terms. He said that the two governments are in general agreement, that we are pressing on with surveys, that further work will be considered with a view to agreed action in accordance with the results of studies, surveys, tests and exercises that are under way or that may be undertaken.
I feel that that was a rather halfhearted response to the stirring exhortation by President Eisenhower that now was the time for action. Therefore I am prompted to ask

The Address-Mr. Pearkes these questions:	Are there any agreed
measures being held in abeyance? If so, why? Alternatively: Are there any measures which are now held in abeyance upon which agreement should be reached without further delay? I have in mind various questions regarding the standardization of arms and equipment.
I suggest that the house is entitled to a further statement as to the precise meaning of General Eisenhower's exhortation. I am sure that that must have been discussed before at government levels.
I thought that the minister might also have touched upon the vital question of manpower. It will be recalled that on February 5, 1951, the minister announced the government's 15-point, 3-year program. The details were given in the white paper of that year and in part III, dealing with manpower, the following appears:
To carry through plans for the next three years the strengths of the three services should be increased to more than 115,000 full-time service personnel.
Recruiting towards this number has progressed favourably so that it is anticipated that the goal will be reached well before the end of the three-year period.
During the first six months of 1951 there has been a net increase of 18,289 in the strengths of the three services, or an average of 3,048 per month. The recruiting program, which began in August 1950 with the enlistment of the special force and which was continued in May 1951 with the raising of the 27th brigade group, will be continued.
At that time I questioned whether the goal of 115,000 men could possibly man the ships and fill up the establishments of the three services as outlined in the program. I believe that subsequently the total was raised to 120,000 personnel. The most recent figures I have, those of October 31 of this year, show the total in the services at the present time as being 106,595. As far as I can gather from the various returns which have been made, the intake now hardly exceeds the discharges. According to the quotation I have just made from the white paper of 1951, the total increase in the first six months of that year in the forces was 18,289. During the last six months of 1953 the total increase has been only 3,000 which was just about the average of one month during those first six months of 1951.
I think the minister should have told us what steps the government are taking, if any, other than to raise the pay of the forces as recently announced, in order to reach the objective which was set when this program was first announced. I would ask: Have we reached the point of saturation? Is there a shortage of manpower of military age in this country? According to a press release


issued by the national advisory council on manpower on November 5, 1953, it would appear that there should be no great shortage. This reads in part:
Over-all manpower supplies were generally adequate to meet the demands of the defence program, of resource development projects, and of expanding civilian industries. The required increase in the labour force was possible chiefly because of an increase in the population aged 14 and over, estimated at 540,000 during the three years ending at June, 1953.
Last Thursday the minister referred to major research projects and to new equipment which is being subjected to the most comprehensive tests. The question is frequently asked: To what extent will new weapons lessen our manpower requirements and to what extent may we expect a reduction in our taxes as a result of the introduction of these new weapons?
Although one might reasonably expect that new weapons would reduce the requirements for the conventional forces, the minister did not give us the slightest indication of any reduction in costs or even of any reduction in the conventional forces. Of course new weapons are costly. This being so, it only underlines the necessity for the strictest economy being exercised wherever possible.
In the recent past I have felt that greater care might have been exercised in expenditures on some of our defence projects. I have found no reason to change my opinion that unless strict economy is exercised in connection with all our defence expenditures we shall only play into the hands of the Soviet communists by placing intolerable strains upon our economy.
Already important social and economic projects have been deferred as a result of expenditures for defence. If our armed forces are to remain effective they must receive the wholehearted support of the nation. When, after years of retrenchment, of heavy taxation and the outpourings of millions of dollars unselfishly given by our people during the years of the war, taxpayers are asked to continue making these sacrifices in more peaceful times, they may become discouraged and withdraw that support if waste and extravagance are noticeable. A balance must be reached as between our military and social requirements that will make us at once secure against external attack and internal destruction. I cannot overemphasize the need for care in all defence spending.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the third member to take his seat in this house representing the people of Comox-Alberni within the memory of any of the members of the house, with the exception I believe of the hon. member fox Quebec

South (Mr. Power), I feel it would not be amiss if I were to make at the outset one or two brief references to my predecessors from Comox-Alberni.
Since coming to Ottawa I have discovered that the high personal regard and friendly relationship that I enjoyed with Mr. Jack Gibson, who I knew principally of course as a political opponent, is very widely shared by the members of this house. I am sure that all hon. members would join with me in wishing Mr. Gibson well in the future. I shall have no objections, Mr. Speaker, to maintaining, in some respects at least, the independent tradition which has long characterized the Comox-Alberni riding. In fact, I should not be at all surprised if there are occasions when some of the members on the opposite side of the house feel that I am perhaps a little more of an independent, as far as they are concerned, than was my predecessor.
I would like to refer to Mr. Neill, who sat in this house as the member for Comox-Alberni from 1921 to 1945. I am sure he is well remembered by all the older members in the house and I am sure they will be interested to know that he recently celebrated his eighty-fifth birthday, in reasonably good health for a man of his years, amid the congratulations of his fellow citizens and all the city councils in the area in which he lives. He still takes a very keen and active interest in the debates in this house and in the public affairs of the country generally.
There are several matters, Mr. Speaker, which I would like to bring to the attention of the house and which are of particular interest and concern to that part of Canada from which I come. But before I do so I would like to refer to something which in my opinion has a significance in the province of British Columbia at the present time, that extends beyond the boundaries of my constituency. It is a situation that vitally affects the whole interior of the province of British Columbia.
The other day a question was asked in the house regarding the present tie-up of the mining industry in Ontario and Quebec and at that time the minister concerned replied that he was not doing anything about that situation. I presume that if the question to which I am now about to refer was raised in the same way his reply would be similar. Nevertheless, I feel that the members of the house should be made aware of a situation which affects the whole of the interior of British Columbia and which affects the production of approximately one-third of the lumber produced in the province.
The whole of the lumber industry in the interior of British Columbia is virtually at a standstill because of a strike which is now 83276-30
The Address-Mr. Barnett in progress in that area, and I feel that hon. members should have some idea of the background to that situation. I think they should realize that it is not something which has come into being overnight, but a situation which has been built up over the period of the last two or three years. It has reached the point where the workers in that industry came to the conclusion that they have no recourse but to take the action they have taken.
I would like hon. members to recognize that the predominant element among the employers in the lumber industry in the interior of British Columbia appear, in my opinion, to be still living in the nineteenth century as far as their attitude to labour management relations is concerned. I could quote, if I wished to take the time, some rather pointed examples of that. But for the moment I would like to draw briefly to the attention of the house one or two excerpts from a statement which came into the hands of the I.W.A. Perhaps I should explain for the benefit of some members of the house, possibly some of them sitting fairly close to me, that in British Columbia I.W.A. stands for International Woodworkers of America and not international wheat agreement.
This document that I have before me is a photostatic copy of a communication which accidentally came into the hands of the union. At the top it is marked "Highly confidential. Important. Please read carefully." At the bottom above the signature it is marked "Keep this bulletin confidential. We must not allow the union to become informed of our strategy."
The document in fact gives instruction to the employers concerned as to how they might go about dealing with their recalcitrant employees, and it states:
Most, if not all, action will probably involve picketing. Under the law persons may locate themselves anywhere outside a private property to "impart information" to anyone, but the actions of such person or persons determine the extent to which such person or persons are obeying or breaking the law.
Then a little later on-I will not read this whole document, but this to me is rather significant-it says:
In the case of pickets appearing before an operation that voted against strike, in addition to all the above, try to have pickets admit that they are picketing, or that it is a picket line-name person or persons who made the statement (It is important to get the admittance that it is a picket line-if necessary get into an argument to get the admittance).
Mr. Speaker, I have quoted from that document in order to illustrate the attitude that has been over a period of years and is now being taken by the employing interests in

The Address-Mr. Barnett the interior of British Columbia. I should like to suggest that the situation is thrown in marked contrast by the fact that right in the centre of the strike area there is today operating at full capacity and peacefully a plywood plant where the employers took the position that they wanted to sit down and to reach an agreement in a reasonable fashion with their employees, and where the union which has the rest of the interior struck at the present time sat down and wrote a long-term agreement with that particular firm. The only interest the employees of that plant have in the strike is the fact that each man in that plant is making every month a substantial contribution to the support of his fellow employees in less fortunate situations.
From time to time I have heard made statements that the union to which I happen to belong and also other unions take a most unreasonable and unrealistic position. I would not argue that that has necessarily never been the case. After all, unions are made up of human beings and sometimes human beings can be unreasonable in any walk of life. Nevertheless I think this situation of unreasonableness is brought out, in a way which makes it clear that it is not always on one side, by this statement which appears here. One of the things that unions have sometimes suggested is that if unions have more factual information on which to reach their conclusions as to what would be a reasonable basis for settlement of disputes, possibly some of the industrial strikes which we experience from time to time could be avoided. This to me at least points up that very fact. It says:
Clumsy efforts of Northern Interior Lumbermen's Association-
This, I should explain, is a publication put out by the union, in case you might think it is something from the operators that I have gotten hold of. The quotation continues:
-to fool the public regarding alleged production losses were neatly exposed last week by the IWA, leaving the operators with scarlet faces.
A full page advertisement in the Prince George Citizen, October 19. over the signature of the association, headed "Where are our Profits?", professed to be an analysis of production and marketing costs based on the average 1,000 board foot unit.
The calculation made placed the net loss to the mill on each 1,000 board foot unit as $10.83.
This announcement was found surnrising to all those with knowledge of the marked increase in production and shipments which has occurred during the past two years. It seemed incredible that production and shipments should have been stepped up. if the looses claimed had been actual.
The advertisement closed with the following statement:

"These figures can be substantiated by examination of actual records and documents, and any person or group desirous of so doing is invited to visit our office".
As the most interested group, the IWA district policy committee immediately took advantage of the offer, for the committee was prepared to consider the true facts as a guide to future action.
Accordingly, the firm of Griffiths & Griffiths, chartered accountants, was retained and representatives of that firm journeyed to Prince George, with instructions to get the facts, as promised by the association.
