Mr. Speaker, I will not dwell on that matter any further at this time; but when there exists a situation which affects as seriously as that situation does such a wide section of the province, I do feel that this house should be aware of some of the facts pertaining to it.
To come a little closer to home, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote frpm an editorial which appeared in the West Coast Advocate published in Port Alberni on November 19 last. It says:
It is gratifying at this time to learn that the federal government has advanced its program to construct an addition to its local assembly wharf . . .

At the present time also the federal government is calling for tenders for improvements to the boat basin at French creek...
From these two projects alone it can be seen that Ottawa is not forgetting the west coast even though it did not return one of their party members.
Mr. Speaker, I would not presume to occupy the attention of the house with that reference were it not for the concluding sentence. As far as I am concerned, the particular projects mentioned are normal expansion of government services. It appears to me that the inference therefrom is that it is clearly a matter of surprise on the part of the publisher of that paper that these services continue even though a member of the government party was not returned. It is almost as if the publisher of this paper-who incidentally was the Liberal candidate in the last election-half expected the members of the government to act as arbitrary, autocratic and narrowly partisan individuals prepared to wreak their vengeance on the hapless constituents of any riding that presumed not to return one of their members to parliament. As far as I am concerned I should like to make it clear that I have some confidence that events will prove the publisher of this paper to be wrong in that assumption. As the member for Comox-Alberni, I shall proceed on the assumption that ministers of the crown are interested in extending the benefits of normal government services equally to all Canadians.
I do not intend to dwell at any length upon the glories of the Comox-Alberni constituency. The only remark I would make in that connection is that I believe we have a considerably greater mileage of seashore than, I would say, all the constituencies of Alberta and Saskatchewan put together. Nevertheless, the miles of rugged seacoast, the long inlets, the mountain ranges and the numerous islands do create some problems which may or may not exist in other parts of Canada. One of these, Mr. Speaker, is in the matter of elections.
I recall that in one of the earlier sittings in this session the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), in reply to a question, said that he was aware of no widespread disfranchisement. Perhaps in a narrow, legal sense the Prime Minister is correct in that most of the people in Canada who were eligible to vote had an opportunity of getting their names on the voters' list. But what, in actual fact, did happen on August 10? I should like to give one illustration. In the city of Port Alberni there are three industrial plants of roughly equal size employing between 500 and 800 men. Normally these plants close for the summer vacation period on a staggered 8327G-30J
The Address

Mr. Barnett basis each year. It happened that one of these plants had its annual two-week shutdown period at the time the federal election took place. While most of these people were on the voters' list, I submit that they had a choice of either forfeiting their right to the ballot or forfeiting their right to their annual holidays.
I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is not a fair choice or a democratic choice to place before the citizens of this country. As I understand it, that situation existed in a great many parts of Canada. If it were a purely passing situation, due entirely to the timing of last summer's election, I might not be disposed to raise the matter now. So far as Comox-Alberni is concerned, however, that situation occurs every time there is a federal election because of the way in which the election act is drawn. Hundreds of the voters in that area have a choice between bread and the ballot, because of the nature of the constituency and the nature of the work which the people in that area do.
I am prepared to agree that the technical changes in the election act are properly matters for the chief electoral officer. I could not agree, nor do I think many members of this house would agree, that the principles behind our federal election act are not properly the concern of this parliament. Great expense is undertaken in some instances in order to give people the right to vote under the present act. I have been told that during the election last summer four-engine airplanes were employed to take the ballot boxes thousands of miles so that a few people could vote. I have no quarrel with that. I submit, Mr. Speaker, however, that it should not be beyond the power of reasonable men to draw that act in such a way that loggers and fishermen may have the opportunity of voting at every election.
It seems to me that what creates this dilemma for people in such occupations is that the act, as it is now drawn, gives priority to the matter of residence rather than to the matter of citizenship. Today we live in an age of movement, and the residence we occupy from time to time may be purely incidental to the occupation we are following. I have some ideas as to how that act might be amended in order to cope with the needs of fishermen and loggers. From what I have been told by some of these people I would say they have ideas, too. Some of the loggers I know resort to the old principle of hedging.
I was discussing with some of them the problem they would face if the particular logging camp in which they were working happened to close down for the fire season a

The Address-Mr. Barnett week before the election. This is a common occurrence in every federal election. When the camp closes the loggers have to go to Vancouver, and their board and lodging ceases when the work ceases. Many of them said to me, "Oh, we fixed that. We had the old lady put our name on the voters' list at home, and we did the same thing up here. We are protected whichever way the thing goes." I did not take the time to explain that such procedure might involve them in some conflict with some sections of the act. Nevertheless I think it does indicate that these people were genuinely interested in having the opportunity to vote. Certainly they had no intention of abusing the privilege.
I shall have to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I made one pledge, and only one pledge, to the people of Comox-Alberni. I said that if I had to make a nuisance of myself in Ottawa for the entire period of this parliament, I would certainly continue to press for some suitable revision of the election act.
Another matter which I should like to draw to the attention of the house and the government is the situation which exists with respect to communications in that area, particularly as it applies to the government telegraph and telephone service. From my travels I have gradually come to the conclusion that for some reason or other the government telephone and telegraph services must be the Cinderella of government departments. The whole pattern of equipment, and the whole set-up, seems to be a carryover from the days of the trail of '98, when if I recall correctly they built a land line to the Yukon.
This matter was drawn rather forcefully to my attention, and I believe also to the attention of the minister in charge last summer, by a situation that developed on one of the islands in the strait of Georgia. I shall quote briefly from one of the communications I have had in this connection. As it happened this island was connected by marine cable, and something happened to this cable with the result that these people were left without telephone service for more than a month before the cable could be repaired. I am not being particularly critical of that situation, because it may have developed accidentally. The communication says:
Our problem does not start nor end with repairs to the marine cable. Practically no useful maintenance work has been done on the land line for the past five years. This land line consists of 12 miles of rusted wire supported by rotting poles which have been in for 25 years, none of them now fit to climb, and many of them with insulators gone, and the line either lying in the ditch or shorted on limbs of trees. We maintain that if


this line was an essential service 25 years ago it is much more essential today as we have had exactly the same mail service for the past 30 years and no improvement in it at any time since.
That, to me, does illustrate a situation which, as I know from my observation, is not confined to that immediate vicinity. That is something which I feel should not continue to exist in an area which is not in the midst of a dying economy. If the people were moving out of the northern end of Vancouver island and the adjacent islands there might be some excuse for letting a service of that kind die away. But I should like to point out that virtually an industrial revolution has taken place in that area in the last ten years, and that in the course of that time there have been three or four huge feudal empires of modern industrialism set up there, so that virtually the whole northern end of the island is now divided up between them.
I realize that this is partly because of forestry policies followed by the present and previous governments in British Columbia. Nevertheless, there it is; new communities are going in, and the people who are producing in those industries are living in the communities.
I am not now suggesting that the government of Canada should attempt to do anything about that situation. I think it is going to take something more than silk-hat socialists to do very much about it. But the thing I do want to point out is that while this communications system is being let fall into a state of decay, these new communities are being left without the facilities afforded by proper, public communications channels, and that comes very close to the question of the rights of free speech and free communication.
I could tell the house of instances where prearranged code words have had to be brought into existence between parties so they could enjoy free communication, because such facilities as there are have been the private concern of the industrialists. I would submit that while this government may not be prepared to do anything about the economic situation, or to do anything about creating a state of industrial democracy, at least it is in accordance with the best traditions of the Liberal party, as I understand them, that the rights of free speech and free communication should be protected and developed.
I think my suggestion is somewhat in line with one made the other day by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) in relation to post office facilities. I should like to draw to the attention of the government

the importance of giving some proper consideration to the development and improvement of this government telephone and telegraph service.
There is one other matter I should like to mention briefly, and that has to do with transportation in the coastal areas of British Columbia. We have a situation now where, almost without notice, steamer services are being withdrawn or reduced. People are worrying. Those who have been on the islands for the last thirty years or more are suddenly left without the means of getting in their supplies. We have up the west coast of Vancouver island, and to all those isolated communities, what amounts to a most unsatisfactory steamer service.
Of course we cannot overlook the impact of air travel upon the facilities that can be provided by a coastal steamship service. Certainly no one would suggest that the advantages of air travel should be removed from those people. It seems to me a revolution is taking place in the whole transportation set-up in that coastal area. I draw this to the attention of the house because I believe it is a matter to which the government should be giving very careful study and attention at this time.
There is a need for the development of an over-all and co-ordinated policy in respect of the type of services that can be supplied to and maintained for the people on the coast. I think some study must be made as to how those services can be co-ordinated, keeping in mind possible highway developments which, of course, would involve some form of study in respect of the authority of the provincial government.
This is a most important matter for those people who live in communities separated from each other by arms of the sea or by mountain ranges, and who should have regular communications with the outside world. So I am asking that this matter receive more consideration and study by the appropriate government departments, so people will have some confidence that they are not going to be suddenly left without adequate transportation facilities.
And while we are on the subject of transportation I should like to suggest that this matter of a coastguard service on the west coast of Vancouver island, and along the west coast generally, is not something which should be brushed aside lightly, as the minister appeared to do the other day when the matter was raised. The two lifeboat stations to which he referred are located a relatively few miles apart on one section of that coast, and certainly are not to be considered as being in the class of a proper coastguard
The Address-Mr. Studer service. I would not suggest that they de not perform or have not performed at times a necessary and useful function, but certainly they are not performing the function of a coastguard service as we understand it.
In closing I should like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to the attention of the house, the fact that even in the prosperous coast lumber industry at the present time there is a situation developing which has a ring rather similar to that raised with respect to other industries such as coal mining and textiles, and with regard to the surpluses of wheat. Just recently some 700 of the plywood workers of the British Columbia coast were laid off. When they will go back to work I do not know. I thought it would be of some interest to the house to know the reason which has been given for that lay-off, in a release by the company concerned. The release is from MacMillan and Bloedel Limited. It says:
Due to expanding Canadian economy, the company in 1951 laid plans for increased producing capacity which might come into effect in 1953. But completion of these facilities, and the engagement of larger crews to increase production, coincided with a wheat policy in Canada, whereby delay has occurred in selling a big part of the 1953 crop to Britain.
Whereas for many years past, fall and winter purchasing power for plywood and other products has been supported by a wide distribution of cash for grain, this year the prairie farmer's available funds from the current crop are much reduced. Plywood buying is being delayed there and elsewhere in Canada to such an extent that the expected increased demand in the fall season has not occurred this year.
I should like to draw this to the attention of the house as some indication of how closely the welfare of the people in one part of Canada is tied to that of the others. I for one, as a member from the coastal area of British Columbia, am quite prepared to take an interest in what some of my colleagues from the central part of this country say to us about wheat.
Thank you.

We have heard reference made to the quota system and the irregularities and the discriminations and what-have-you that occur under it. Much of that may be due to the use of quota books. Last year it was worked on the basis of the wheat acreage only instead of the total acreage. This year the quota is on a new basis of three bushels per total acreage, and that will eliminate many of the discrepancies that formerly existed. There have been difficulties as between one point and another in connection with the box cars allotted over a period of the past years.
Then they talk about the car order book removal. I think everyone will agree that if the wheat board has an order for wheat, whatever grade it may be, it must obtain that wheat at whatever point it is possible to obtain it. Otherwise it will lose the sale. What good would it do to interfere with the selling of certain grades of wheat? The wheat board is out to sell wheat and nothing else. If it does not sell wheat the farmers of western Canada are going to suffer.
I would not interfere one iota with the operations of the wheat board, because they are the men who know how to sell wheat. I do not think any socialists anywhere in the country could have sold one particle more than they have sold. They are partial to socialist countries, but socialist countries are getting scarcer and scarcer so they would have considerable difficulty in the sale of wheat.
Let us look at what happens when there is no quota. Our friends refer to the United States quite often. I was down in the United States at a shipping point where there were from 150 to 200 trucks lined up on a Sunday waiting for the whistle of a train. The minute that train pulled in there was a scramble to get to the elevator to deliver their wheat. At least we have a quota system which brings about some semblance of order in the delivering of our wheat. I think we should continue it and increase our efforts to make it equitable for all concerned.
There should not be this constant sniping at the wheat board which we hear throughout Canada and in this House of Commons. It just does not make sense. I believe that our socialist friends would like nothing better than to have the wheat board operations collapse. The government of this country operated this wheat board against the wishes of more than 93 per cent of the people. How many people in Canada, apart from some of the wheat-growing farmers in western Canada, and not all of them, wanted the wheat board? Did the people of British Columbia want it?

I never heard them say so. Did the people east of the great lakes want it? I did not hear them say so. I do not think any socialists in any part of this country wanted it. They would not have been able to handle it if they had tried to do it.
If you have the government of Canada enhancing the position of the western farmers, even against opposition to the setting up of the very wheat board that was brought into operation for the well-being of the farmer, then why the continual sniping in regard to it? I think we should give our government a vote of gratitude, not only the people of British Columbia but the people of Canada as a whole. These people who keep sniping and contradicting and discussing and arguing about it are rendering a disservice to the people of Canada and thereby to the farmers of western Canada by the action they have taken up to date.
We also hear something about cattle. We have them talking about a crisis in this regard. In fact I have never heard anything discussed by the socialists in this house that was not a crisis. Even if cattle were 38 cents a pound it would still be a crisis. Most of them talk about crises and if they continue in that vein they will be in a perpetual crisis. They want a livestock marketing board, but the livestock growers do not want it. They passed resolutions against it and they told me not to support it because it would lead to controls and they do not want control in regard to cattle. Socialists want it because their whole system is based on controls, on control of every part of the economy, including people. The cattle growers can see through that flimsy argument the socialists continue to present, and the cattlemen would rather set up their own board than have a state-controlled system. They do not want controls and directions designating whether they might sell one head or one thousand head of cattle.
The same thing holds true of production in other fields. In any event, if the socialists are in favour of controls then let them go to the province of Saskatchewan. Let the provincial government build the storage and refrigeration that will be necessary for livestock. Let the socialist government wake up from their sleep and endeavour to provide the storage that will be necessary for that produce. If the province has to provide it, then perhaps they can encourage them to do so in the same way the people of Canada have provided similar marketing facilities for the smaller growers of livestock in this country. They have never made any effort before.

They had a natural products marketing act which they did pass, but it was bypassed out in Saskatchewan.
As I said last year, there is not one single instance in which the socialists have made an effort to help the farmers and the people in the west. They have confined themselves to criticizing the federal government from which all the revenue comes into Saskatchewan, and which has accrued through the operations of the farming industry during the past years.
We have heard many speeches from socialist members in the House of Commons, but they all play the same record. It is the same tune, although now it is a little scratchier. It is still the same record about what we are going to do in regard to cattle and farming conditions generally. But are we going to accept what they say about the actual situation in Saskatchewan? Are we going to accept what they have told us, that the situation in Saskatchewan is worse than ever before, and that there is a continual crisis there at the present time? I suggest they go and talk to the provincial treasurer instead of giving us this gloom-doom socialism. The provincial treasurer has this to say on page 7 of his budget speech for this year:
Despite these danger points, and the setbacks I have mentioned, it still remains true that 1952 has been the most prosperous farm year in our history. The gross value of agricultural production is estimated at well over $1 billion, an all-time high by a wide margin. Actual cash income received during the year rose to $700 million. And while net farm income for the country as a whole fell by 12 per cent from the 1951 record, this province registered a gain of better than 10 per cent.
I have not too much faith in the provincial treasurer out there, but I still have more faith in his words than I have in the humdrum speeches I have heard here this session.
On page 11 the statement continues:
Finally, the data on personal income provides the key to the story of Saskatchewan's expanding economy.
Where did this expansion in Saskatchewan's economy come from? Not from oil. They have realized on that, but only incidentally. It comes from the soil and the produce of the farms, from the overwhelming production of agriculture and livestock products, and from the wheat and other grains of western Canada. The provincial treasurer continues:
As I noted before, the estimate just published at Ottawa places personal income for Canada as a whole in 1952 at $17,146 billion. This is $1,188 per capita. A preliminary estimate for Saskatchewan is $1-210 billion. This is $1,435 per capita- 70 per cent higher than the previous ten-year average, and one-fifth better than the national average.
The Address-Mr. Studer
His statement should be accepted as an indication of the real situation in Saskatchewan. That is not the situation as a whole out west but it is certainly the situation as a whole in Saskatchewan, and it contradicts what has been said in this house by the socialists. But are they dismayed? No, they are not; even when the provincial treasurer, even when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in a speech the other day, and even when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) proved that they had not a leg to stand on. They are not dismayed as long as they have a soft spot to sit on. They sit in the house twiddling their tongues, and when they are not twiddling their tongues they are twiddling their thumbs and waiting for the day when they will receive pensions as members of this house.
I would venture this statement, and I would like to have someone contradict it. We have had the best years in this country when there were no socialists in the House of Commons whatsoever. They have always been a detriment to every country in which they have lived. We hear their arguments in regard to the percentage of national wealth. Perhaps we do not have a fair percentage qf national wealth in southwestern Saskatchewan, but when they take the figures from the record to prove that the farmer is not receiving a fair percentage of the national wealth, they do not take all the figures. They just take part of them.
I do not say the farmers are getting their share of the national wealth. I do not think they are, but the people I know who are getting a fair percentage of the national wealth are the socialists in the government of Saskatchewan. I think they are getting their share of the national wealth.
In any event no one will agree that the farmers are getting their fair percentage of the national wealth. The farmers will not agree, nor will the fishermen, the miners and the industrial workers. I would say, though, that it must be fairly equal at the present time because no one seems to be in a position to prove they are not receiving their fair share of the national wealth. I think we can take it as a compliment to the government, which has distributed the wealth better than any other government throughout the length and breadth of this country.
If the situation in Saskatchewan in regard to credit is bad, one of the best things they could do would be to close the liquor stores, which took in over $32 million last year; and if they did close them, in many localities it would increase the well-being and economic condition of the people in that province.

The Address-Mr. Studer
We are free traders out west and I think something should be done about that by the dominion government. I think we should take the duty off cement, because we are in a hazardous situation in that part of the country. Although the duty is not heavy, enough is involved to make a considerable impact upon prices. If we could have more cement at lower prices the situation would be improved considerably and we could make a recommendation to the province of Saskatchewan that they take the 3 per cent tax off building, particularly where the homes of the poor are involved. They place a 3 per cent tax on building the homes of the poor in Saskatchewan.
Oh, more than that, Mr. Speaker. They place a 3 per cent tax on the building of hospitals, the cost of which is contributed to by the Dominion of Canada on a percentage basis. Those humanitarians out there impose a tax on the dominion government that itself supplies a percentage of the cost of building of hospitals out there. Take the duty off cement; take the duty off cars and trucks; take the duty off farm tires and let us get back to a free trade basis. 1 never heard of anything in connection with tariffs that did not shackle the western Canadian farmer. If we are going to assist him, that is one little way in which we can try to do it.
Our farmers have to meet competition. Let none of you easterners think you are underwriting the wheat of western Canada. We have an international wheat agreement, and it is underwritten by the people signing that international wheat agreement as to the minimum and also as to the maximum. No one in Canada is in danger of having to come to the support of the western wheat growers at the present time; and no one has done so at any time very much, in spite of the $65 million that we have heard too much about in this country of ours. Place us in a position where we are not handicapped and shackled with these tariffs, so we can operate and produce out there on a basis of equality with other people. I have 200 miles of Montana border down there. I know what it costs on one side and what it costs on the other.
I make no apologies for being a free trader not only in this matter but in everything that goes into production. The whole world will be better off when we get into a position of absolute free trade and not just free trade between certain countries.
Don't worry about the farmers being too rich out in western Canada. The only way you are going to get rich, if you have ambitions that way, is to see that the farmer gets rich first. Incidentally, if there is any standard of living in this country, who should 
have it? Who is the first one that has a right to it, if it is not the primary producer who produces the food? He is the one who should have the highest standard of living in this country, not the lowest. He should not be forced to take that which is left after everyone else has had a portion of it or has taken what he thought was his just due. The primary producer on the farm and in the factory, the labourers and the fishermen and all those who produce that which is essential to life, should have the highest standard of living. But no one in this house will say they have had it. I think we should concentrate our efforts on achieving that end.
There are other things happening in the west that should have our attention. Not only is there the wheat crisis but there are other crises. One is the crisis in the political situation in the west. Here we have companies going into western Canada selling their products of all descriptions. But what has happened? They were interested only in the selling of goods. They were never interested in selling themselves to the people of Canada. If they are to be of any value to this country whatsoever, then along with the sale of their products they had better begin selling themselves.
You see what has happened out in western Canada which is the paradise of political opportunists who will take every advantage of that situation, be it in opposition to eastern Canada, telling the people that all of eastern Canada is against them. Eastern Canada has not sold itself out in western Canada either, with the result that out of 70 members we have 23 here in the House of Commons representing the government. Oh, the west may be necessary economically but politically it is expendable. I think the people of Canada should know that.
Here in the House of Commons we have a socialist group from the west, from Saskatchewan, who contribute nothing to the welfare of Canada except contradiction and opposition. All of them should be put together, all these opposition parties, and they should be called the "protestionist" party of Canada. I think that is necessary in more ways than one.
They are talking about reform of the Senate -excuse me, Mr. Speaker; I should say reform of the other place. I will talk about a few reforms here in the House of Commons. We can start with the splinter parties. If ever there was a waste of time in any parliament in any country in the world, it has been in this House of Commons. When the time comes that parliament should be closed I have to sit here and listen to people who have nothing else in the world to do except make their living by talking and

being members of the House of Commons. I think something should be done about it. Why is it that the small percentage of the people of Canada represented by the socialists, as they were in the last parliament-I think it is 6 per cent of the people of Canada -should be able to create this situation? Their representatives, the socialists, absorbed over 30 per cent of the time of this House of Commons, and they represented 6 per cent of the people.
I think we need some co-ordination in the House of Commons. I think we should place our splinter parties in the position where they will group themselves together with the official opposition party or be criticized continually for never wanting to be the government. I do not think they want to be the government. I think they are perfectly content to remain in splinter groups for the rest of their lives, because it is a better living than I know some of us make out in the country working in the way we are working. They are a voice crying in the wilderness. I think they should co-ordinate the political voice of the west. If the Social Crediters cannot convince the C.C.F.'ers, whom are they going to convince? And if the socialists cannot convince the Social Crediters, whom are they going to convince? Of course the Conservatives convince no one, so they are all in the same boat. I would suggest that these political splinter parties be not recognized in this House of Commons until such time as they have 25 per cent of the vote in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the real crisis is out in Saskatchewan. They speak about this thing called communism. They ask what causes communism, and they say hunger causes communism. I could perhaps believe that when I look at the physique of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles); but when I look at the constitution of the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) and the well-fed,
468	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Studer ready-for-market constitution of the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Ellis) I would say, as would my Scottish friends, "I hae ma doots". If they are in that position, and are proud to be socialists, of what are they proud? Where in the world did a socialist ever make a contribution to anything? It is the easiest thing in the world to be a socialist. They seem to consider that you have to have some superhuman ideology or thought in order to be a socialist.
It is, however, the easiest thing in the world to be a socialist. All that needs to happen is for me to have a crop failure, then for the cattle to get hoof-and-mouth disease, the hogs to get hog cholera, the chickens to get coccidiosis; then love flies out the window and the wife leaves home. After everything is gone I say "Boys, I have had it; hooray, I am a socialist and willing to share everything I have not got with everything you have got". I question these individuals as to their right to be socialists. I do not think any non-wealth producing individual has a right to be a socialist. These socialists question us as to our right to be capitalists. Do they not question every capitalist as to his right to be a capitalist, implying that everyone got to be a capitalist by robbing the poor?
In all cases they are against any individual and any country that is doing good, any country that has been able to produce more and distribute more than any other country on the face of the earth, including Canada. Last year I questioned some of them as to their right to be socialists. I have as much right to question them about their right to be socialists as they have to question me about my right to be a capitalist-that would be a laugh for my creditors. I have a right to question them as to why a non-wealth-producer has a right to be a socialist. They may say the members of the government are nonproducers, and that may be true; but the difference is, those members are not socialists.
I am asking these socialists where they got their right to be socialists. Did they get it from God? No, they did not, because God knows you have to be a producer before you can distribute anything. Did they get it from Karl Marx or from Engels? No; they also were non-producers. Did they get it from nature? No, because the bees in the beehive make short shrift of the drone. Did they get it from the people? No, because they were socialists before the people ever heard of them. From what source did they get this right to be a socialist? My time is not up as yet, so I will give any one of these nonwealth-producing socialists three minutes to tell me from what source they got this right to be a socialist. Proceed.


Well, it appears as though they were unable to substantiate it. If they cannot substantiate it, then the folks out in western Canada ought to know they have been political impostors. I am going to jolt, jab, prod, dig, abuse, ask and argue until I eliminate these impostors.
Who solved the problem of production? Not the socialists, because if we had started off with their policy we would still be the underprivileged people of the world. We would not have to talk about distribution, we would be talking about producing something to eat. The same thing holds true all along the line. They never solved the problem of production, yet they take it unto themselves, by divine right, to say they are going to distribute my labour, my toil, and my sweat. They have no right to it. I have the right to the things I produce from my sweat and toil, not those socialists.
If they say they are delivering a service and they are educationists or ministers, let them go out and distribute that throughout the country. I am telling the people of Canada this, it is germ warfare. It is germ warfare because these reprehensible specimens of socialist bacteria are spreading their germ warfare all over the people of Canada, taking advantage of the weak and underprivileged and those who may have no access to knowledge and education.
My time is almost up, so I shall not be able to go into the subject matter of my speech. In closing I would ask the government not to overlook the poor; do not take it for granted that all is well in Canada. Yet there are more people enjoying the good things of life in Canada, enjoying a higher standard of living, with more future and more freedom than in any socialist country in the world. I am going to do my part to try to keep it so. Let not the government for a minute consider or believe that we have a perfect government or that we should be arrogant-which the government is not. The duty of the government is to its people. The Liberal government does not wrong the rights, as the socialists do; the government rights the wrongs, and that is what we shall endeavour to do in the future. We shall so operate the economy that people of all classes have an opportunity to earn their living, as is their right.
Although we are happy that so many people in Canada enjoy the benefits of our civilization, some of us are still unhappy because there are some who do not enjoy those benefits. Our policy shall be that everyone shall have the right to earn his living, that is everyone who wishes to do so, in order to ensure that our country will become great. I believe

this government has the best system and the best policies to sustain the right of every individual to provide the highest standard of living within his capacity. All of us will continue to be dedicated to the task of making it possible for all the people of Canada to attain the abundant life.

Sit down, we have had enough of that. We fought the last war in order to get rid of these dictators, these Hitlers in this country. I have not, as I said, the time to answer the hon. member.
There are many important subjects, Mr. Speaker, about which I should like to speak tonight but time will not permit. I should like to speak about agriculture, as that is a very important subject in my constituency. However, other members of the Social Credit party have discussed that subject quite thoroughly during this session. Then I should like to spend some time discussing pensions, as that is a very important subject and one about which a great number of people are deeply concerned. They are concerned about pensions for our senior citizens, pensions for the blind, pensions for veterans and pensions for the disabled. Again, those questions have been dealt with by other members of the Social Credit party, so I shall not bother with them at this time. There will be opportunities later this session when those matters can be discussed.
There is an important subject though, Mr. Speaker, in which my constituents are interested and about which I want to say something this afternoon. I have spoken on this subject on many occasions since I have been a member of this house. I am sorry the government has not seen fit to do much about it. I am referring to the coal industry of western
The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston Canada, not particularly of western Canada but the whole of Canada, because the coal industry is in distress.
The other day the h'on. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) was outlining conditions in the coal industry in his constituency. He pointed out where mines were being closed and miners were losing their jobs, and that the coal industry was going down.
That same condition prevails out in western Canada. I can remember speaking on this subject at the last session, and at that time I gave the number of mines, and their names, in my constituency that had been closed. I put on the record at that time the number of men who had been put out of employment in that constituency, and pointed out that they had nowhere else to go for employment if they wished to remain in that industry.
Yet nothing was done. It is so important a problem that the provincial ministers who have jurisdiction over coal mining in their respective provinces had a meeting at Niagara Falls to discuss the matter. I should like to read an account of what happened at that meeting, as reprinted in the Albertan of September 19, 1953. It is headed "Ask Action to Bolster Sagging Coal Industry". The article is dated Niagara Falls, and purports to be a Canadian Press release, stating:
Provincial governments-
And hon. members will note that the plural is used.
-Friday were urged to ask Ottawa for a clear-cut national policy statement on Canada's coal industry.
The recommendation was made in the report of a committee headed by J. P. Messervey, deputy mines minister of Nova Scotia, and presented at the closing session here of the 10th annual mines ministers conference.
After an examination of the industry's problems in the east and west, the committee received conference backing for further talks between the coal board and the conference's standing committee on coal policy.
It does seem to me the subject is so important that the federal government should take some notice of it. It is so important that each of the provinces is becoming concerned, and it is no longer a provincial matter. It has become a matter for the federal government.
One of my reasons for taking this opportunity to say a few words about the coal industry lies in the fact that perhaps we in Alberta are more distressed by the condition than any other part of Canada-and I am not for one moment minimizing conditions outside Alberta. The fact is, however, that in Alberta we produce one-seventeenth of

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston the world's known supply of coal. Yet our coal industry is being pushed out because of the lack of a Canadian fuel policy.
The position in Alberta is becoming serious because of the development of substitute fuels, in the forms of fuel oil and gas. No one would suggest that it would be desirable to stop the trend of progress, and it would not be wise of course to stop the development of the use of fuel oil and gas. These are things that will bring progress in our country. Gas is to be shipped down here to Ontario. We do ship some coal to this province, and we expect that the shipment of gas here will have some effect on our coal shipments, and upon the coal market generally in eastern Canada.
Then, too, the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterway, providing added power to the central provinces, will have an effect on our coal market in this part of Canada. It is clear, therefore, that we have a problem facing us. Although Alberta, as I said, produces one-seventeenth of the world's supply, in 1952 we produced in that province only 7,150,000 tons. That is only a fraction of our capacity. While the figures are not complete, it is estimated that this year we will produce only 6,260,000 tons or a decrease in production in one year amounting to 890,000 tons. We shipped 597,461 tons to central Canada, mostly to Ontario.
That is not very much for central Canada. Our coal industry is going down. What would have happened to us during the last war if we had had a depleted coal production? The answer is that we would have been in a very serious situation indeed. What will happen to us in another emergency if we have to fall back on the coal industry, only to find there is no coal industry left? Obviously this is a national problem. In Canada last year our total production was only
17.360.000	tons, and it is estimated that for this year we will have an even lower production. In fact the estimate is, by those in the coal business, that it will be the smallest since 1941.
The question may be asked, and quite properly: Well, where is the coal market? The answer is that we have a very good coal market in Canada, the best part of which is found right here in Ontario and Quebec, with the greater proportion in Ontario. As I said a moment ago Canada produced last year 17,360,000 tons, but it must be pointed out that we imported from the United States
24.176.000	tons. We imported 6,816,000 tons more than we produced. Out of the total imports, Ontario brought in from the United States in 1952 an amount totalling 2,215,000 tons, while Quebec imported 1,125,000 tons.


The evidence is clear that there is a market in Canada for Canadian coal. But what has the government done about it? While we have this market it seems to me the height of folly to allow an important industry, such as the Canadian coal industry, to become bankrupt. It is estimated that we could increase our present output by about 4 million tons per year. Alberta could increase her present production to about 10 million tons. In place of that we are now producing
7,150,000	tons.
What does this mean? It means that if we wanted to save the industry all we would have to do would be to find a market here in central Canada for a million tons. That might save the industry. If we could find a market in Ontario for 2 million tons, the industry could be stabilized; and if a market could be found in Ontario and Quebec for 4 million tons the industry could be put back on its feet so those employed in it could have a decent and satisfactory standard of living.
That would not be so hard to do; it would create a hardship on no one. We import over 24 million tons of coal from the United States. If we were to increase our consumption of Canadian-produced coal to the extent of 4 million tons we would still be importing from the United States over 20 million tons, and we would be producing in Canada about the same amount.
No; the federal government will not establish a Canadian coal policy, though they have been asked to do so for many years, and yet that is the crying need. We need a Canadian fuel policy so our people who are in that industry may make a living and that so vital an industry may be maintained. But no; the government which my hon. friend who preceded me lauded so highly could not establish an all-Canadian fuel policy for coal, but they can shout their heads off for a Canadian policy for gas. And what kind of gas? It is Alberta's cheap gas. They even do not want to pay a decent price for it. They want to get our gas down here at a cheap price. They will not take our coal; oh, no. Canada will be subsidizing the St. Lawrence waterway project, but will not establish a coal policy.

I want to refer to the statement by the Prime Minister as reported in the Albertan of Tuesday, July 14, 1953. The article is headed:
Prime Minister commits Liberals to all-Canada gas line.
Edmonton (C.P.)-Prime Minister St. Laurent Monday night pledged the Liberal government to back development of an all-Canadian pipe line to give eastern Canadian centres the benefit of Alberta's cheap natural gas.
Oh, yes, they can establish a national fuel policy in that respect, but who gets the benefit? Ontario and Quebec. Then the article goes on to say:
On the rest of Alberta's exports the Liberal government's policy was "quite clear".
We support fully the proposal that this surplus should go to central and eastern Canada and it is our policy to see to it that this surplus should go to central and eastern Canada by means of an all-Canadian pipe line.
Oh, yes, they are not backward in establishing an all-Canadian policy for Alberta's cheap gas, but they will not do very much to help us out in establishing a Canadian fuel policy for coal, an industry that is so vital to the welfare of this country, an industry that anyone with half an eye can see is going to be ruined unless something is done about it.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) mentioned the gold subsidy. Yes, we can subsidize gold; we have done that. In the period 1948 to 1952 the gold subsidy cost us $59,984,164. Do you know how many people that industry employs? It employs 23,000. We give them $59 million and some odd, nearly $60 million, in a five-year period, yet we cannot add a little bit more to the coal subsidy in order to give thousands upon thousands of miners and their families a decent standard of living. Mr. C. E. Johnston Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I want to start these few remarks by saying how much I rejoice at your nomination to the high post you now fill. In putting your name forward, the government made a wise choice, and your nomination received the approval of all members, regardless of political affiliation. Everyone had taken it for granted, for some time, that you would be called upon to preside over the parliamentary business of this house. You were well prepared for this post and highly able to fill it; your nomination is a tribute to your lability and your already brilliant parliamentary career.
I do not intend to speak at length. If I take part in this traditional debate it is only because I want to express immediately my opinion on certain subjects; besides I never thought that any miracle could be wrought by long and endless speeches. This debate offers a member the opportunity to recite his opinions-which as a matter of fact reflect those of his constituents-to tell the government what those opinions are, and maybe also to be of some help in the final drafting of the bills.

During the present session, the government will introduce a bill to allow more Canadians to acquire their own houses. It is a very commendable program, and those who wish to become home owners await the details with some impatience. The sooner the bill is discussed, the more satisfied people will be. I am bound to state that the public at large, and more particularly those who live outside the larger centres, were not altogether satisfied with the way the present act operates, and my constituents have sent me, on that particular point, complaints which did seem to be justified.
The new measure would reduce the down payment to 10 per cent. This is a tremendous step in the right direction and all the more laudable since the refunding period would be extended. It has been said that banks would be called upon to grant loans; this should be a boon particularly for people residing in small towns or in rural communities.
It will be much easier for them to apply to local branches of banks than it has been to get in touch with the head offices of loan companies or even with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. For, up to now, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the loan companies were rather averse to grant loans outside large centres; they alleged so many reasons for reducing them to the minimum that the claimants, sick and tired of delays and evasive answers, withdrew their applications. For my part, I believe that the housing legislation should apply to all Canadians, no matter where they live, be it in cities, villages or rural districts, as long as they comply with the basic conditions and give the necessary reimbursement guarantees. The National Housing Act will succeed, will attain the purpose envisaged by the government, only if all Canadians are allowed to benefit equally from it.
The hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) has placed on the order paper a resolution concerning the selection of a Canadian flag and has recommended the establishment of a committee to this effect. I do commend him for it. I think, however, that if this committee is ever formed, its first task should be to agree on the principle of an entirely Canadian flag. The design or selection of the design for this flag would then be easy. By an entirely Canadian flag, I mean, as far as I am concerned, a flag containing in its folds no symbol, no sign, no design which recalls either Great Britain or France. The Canadian people originates from two great nations. Canada has been enriched by the qualities of both and, even if we
The Address-Mr. Bertrand should prefer one culture or the other, Canada must be first of all our country. Canada is an adult nation, able to govern itself, and the flag it will choose should prove it. It is not by borrowing from others that we shall affirm our country's power or strengthen the prestige it has gained amongst the nations of the world.
Many groups are recommending the appointment of an ambassador to the Vatican, and my county would approve of such an appointment. I favour it myself, not because I am a Catholic, but because I consider, as a citizen, that the Vatican today is the best listening post and the strongest bulwark against communism. Attacks against the Pope and the Vatican prove this most clearly to be true. Many nations, who have no religious ties with the Vatican, have nevertheless diplomatic relations and consider them essential, absolutely necessary, precisely because the Vatican, apart from the religious question, acts as a barrier against the expansion of the communist doctrine in the world.
In certain quarters, people seem to fear that none but a Catholic could be appointed to this post. There is no strict reason for it and the ambassador might very well be English-speaking and belong to a different religion; I would have no objection to it. The only important thing would be for him to be thoroughly Canadian, well qualified and worthy of the task entrusted to him. Let him be the proud spokesman of Canadians, let him express their aspirations, which consist in upholding the principles of democracy and of the dignity of man, in preserving peace among nations and ensuring their common happiness, as well as in maintaining the cult of our Christian civilization.
I offer the government my heartfelt congratulations for announcing its intention to grant allowances to the handicapped and the disabled. It was on April 1, 1946, that I rose for the first time to speak on a resolution that I had placed on the order paper. This resolution was seconded by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier). Other members such as the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Blanchette), for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) supported this resolution both by further resolutions and in their speeches.
Every year since then it has appeared on the order paper and on March 7, 1951, twenty-six members of the house, from every party, declared themselves in favour of such allowances. No vote could be taken but it was obvious that parliament as a whole was in favour of such a measure. Thousands of

There is much talk about communism. It has been proven that a number of nations are communistic today or sympathize with communism because they have been led to do so by misery and insecurity. But communism has certainly not bettered their condition. They had been promised wonders and an ideal standard of living, but they have only lost their freedom as a nation and have become enslaved.
One must have a minimum of welfare to lead an honest life. The man who steals a small loaf of bread to feed himself or quell the hunger of his family commits an act forbidden by law. It is therefore the duty and the right of society to alleviate misery, because misery is a poor counsellor. We spend enormous sums of money to prepare for war and preserve peace in our country and elsewhere. In fact we are on a war footing. We won the last war but, although it may seem incredible, we have not succeeded in winning peace. Cold war has replaced hot war. Everyone knows the exigencies of cold war; everyone accepts them to avoid the other kind of war which, should it come, would bring chaos to the world and deal a tragic blow to so many nations. Canada is spending the greatest part of its budget in an effort to avoid war; faced with the blunt fact of an ever-possible danger and of an ever-increasing uncertainty towards the future, nations are arming themselves. It seems that the cold war being waged in the world today is far from being over.
Canada devotes huge sums of money and contributes through United Nations agencies to the alleviation of the distressing conditions which still obtain among underprivi-
[Mr Bertrand.1

leged nations; it contributes also to worldwide assistance programs for the benefit of underdeveloped countries; it contributes to all those projects the objectives of which are to relieve misery wherever it may be, to fight these plagues which bring havoc in certain parts of the globe where medicine is still unknown. Nobody finds cause for criticism if these amounts are earmarked for alleviating misery. The alleviation of misery is a direct means of fighting communism. In this country, nobody disapproves of the Family Allowances Act, which helps make better citizens of our youth.
Nobody is opposed to legislating for the benefit of those wounded or handicapped by wars in which they have taken part to defend our country and the civilized world. Nobody is opposed to those laws made to assist old people, blind people or those who require an insurance policy against future risks. There will be unanimous approval for this invalid assistance act. These invalids are outcasts; they are without means, they often are obliged to call upon public charity and their horizon is limited by what they can observe through their window. Helping them is to give them that ray of sunshine that changes into smiles the despair which would otherwise settle upon them.
To abolish misery is to do away with communism. Does communism exist in countries where production is high, salaries good, standards of living high? Does communism take root in a country where the government looks after the hard-working small wage earners, the poor, the sick, the social outcasts? Does communism have a chance to flourish in countries where social security legislation protects the people against the hazards of life and looks after the welfare of those who are in want? And nobody will object, if he is sincere, to paying a few dollars each year in taxes, in order to allow the government of his country to introduce social security legislation which not only helps but ensures internal peace to a nation like ours.
There is, however, a class of society which it would be proper to consider in a special way; I refer to the blind. It may be said that I am indulging overgenerously in social security; that is true. There are certain phases of my life which have left their imprint on my mind and my direct contacts with the people, during the last 25 years, have made me aware of numerous social evils.
I take a special interest in the "Societe Amicale des Aveugles" and, on many occasions, I have received representations from that society. On October 16, an important group of blind people visited this parlia-

ment, and I must thank the clerk of the house, as well as his staff, for having gone to great pains to welcome them properly. It may sound surprising, even if every one was accompanied by a guide, that these blind people were able to visit every nook and cranny of this parliament.
Providence, which does nothing in vain, has endowed the blind with a sensitiveness we do not possess, a sense of perception which we do not have, a way of seeing and picturing things which would surprise us if we could experience it. I think that the blind should not be subjected to the means test, and that the maximum pension should be granted them without any restriction whatsoever.
There are not very many blind people in Canada whose income is large enough to make them self-sufficient. The majority of them cannot live on their monthly allowance, and they have to do some remunerative work.
The blind are not deprived of all their producing capacities, but these capacities are deadened or reduced to nothing. If you want the blind to take on some productive job, you have to make them financially secure. The psychological fear of not being able to keep up their jobs because they might lose their pension if they kept on working adds to their anguish.
When the mining industry, agriculture or some other branch of the national economy is endangered, the government votes grants and subsidies in order to regularize the situation. As far as the blind are concerned, one should try not to destroy the human ideals which dwell in their hearts and make them burn with a brighter flame. The abolition of the means test would ensure their financial, material and moral security. Blindness entails increased expenses for the victims since their cost of living is higher and it is impossible for them to profit from clearance sales; if the blind person wishes to go out, he needs a guide and is often obliged to have guardians at home; more than those who have their sight, the blind may have to face the expenses involved in such wear and tear as the spilling of a liquid, touching a freshly painted surface, and so on. Besides, as blindness is often caused by a poor physical condition or again causes such a condition, drugs and medical attention may involve heavy expenditures.
From the family viewpoint, blindness calls for greater expenses. That is why, in the province of Quebec, 5 per cent of the blind do not receive their pension. The husband or wife of a blind person has to work, for the
The Address-Mr. Bertrand act sets a ceiling on income which, even if the full pension is paid, does not suffice for the upkeep of the family. It often happens that the blind husband takes up residence alone, in order to be able to receive the full amount of the pension, while the burden of working and of bringing up the children falls uipon the wife.
In order to raise the family and social standards and help the blind person maintain his dignity, it is imperative to liberate him from an inferiority complex with respect to those enjoying normal sight.
He lives in darkness; his life is complicated in a hundred ways; he worries and becomes impatient; he feels isolated and forgotten.
I believe that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) would do something worth while if he could supply us with a table showing the number of blind persons per province, the total amount they receive at present and how much more it would cost the nation and the provinces to pay the maximum pension to the blind. We all have blind people in our respective constituencies; would it not be reasonable to try to find a way of improving their lot?
I represent in the house the constituency of Terrebonne, one of the best known tourist areas of the country. Tourist associations, chambers of commerce, tourists' information bureaux and municipal councils spend large sums of money to publicize that part of our country known as the "Canadian Switzerland".
I wonder if the Minister of Resources and Development, under whose jurisdiction comes the Canadian tourist industry and who brings to his new duties both talent and devotion, could not have a study made of the possibility of giving assistance to the tourist associations of this country in their annual publicity campaigns, either by supplying them with publicity material or through grants. I believe that we have here a matter which deserves close consideration.

And I have no objection to other tourist centres in Canada enjoying the same privilege. Documentary films by the national film board are always carefully produced.

It might be objected that there is the matter of income and population. My answer to that is that, in my city, due to special circumstances, there is a particular postal problem which demands a solution in order that the population may get the service to which it is entitled.
My electors have learned with great pleasure that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will undertake shortly a good-will tour of the world. It is my opinion that such a trip will place Canada in a still better light. The Prime Minister is, in fact, thanks to his brilliant personality, a good symbol of the greatness of our country. Canada cannot but gain in increased prestige from this trip. It has no territorial claims to make. It brings to all nations its co-operation, but within the framework of justice. It has but one aim: to serve the cause of peace. To speak on behalf of the Canadian nation and to foster peace and understanding in the world, Canada will have in the person of the Prime Minister an ambassador of the first rank.
Canada, through her domestic and external policies, sets a wonderful example of concord and sincerity. Her delegates to the United Nations are held in high esteem. Last fall I


saw the Hon. Lester Pearson carrying on his work at the United Nations. I could feel his popularity and his reputation. He is a leading diplomat, and the attacks from a few hysterical Americans or their false accusations cannot lessen either here or abroad the reputation of our dynamic Secretary of State for External Affairs. Twice the Hon. Mr. Pearson was spontaneously chosen to be secretary general of the United Nations; twice the delegates from the communist countries prevented his nomination to that high post. His policies, which were those of Canada, stood out clearly; they were the freedom of the people, the defence of the down-trodden, the respect for human and religious rights, and the great fight for peace.
Canada fights for peace in the world and is proud to enjoy peace within her own boundaries. Canada is a great country. She is admired the world over. She believes in democracy and proves it. Canadians, who have full confidence in their democratic system, expect their representatives in parliament not to act in any way which might belittle, lessen, or depreciate that system. They trust the men they have freely chosen to lead their country to new summits and further successes.
I would show ingratitude if I failed today, in this house where I have been sitting these last fourteen years, to address a message of thanks to the people of Terrebonne county who last July gave me such unanimous proof of the confidence they have placed in me.
