Mr. Speaker, I would like, at the outset, to extend to you my congratulations on your election to the office of Speaker of the House of Commons. From what I have seen and heard here, since the beginning of the session, I conclude that we could not have made a better choice.
As you will note, my French is far from perfect; but I do hope that before the end of this parliament, I will be able to speak fluently in your mother tongue, which is the language of my French-speaking colleagues.
(Text):
Second, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my thanks for the very welcome though unexpected assistance I received during the recent election campaign from two members sitting on the front benches opposite me. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), visiting in my riding prior to August 10, had the kindness to tell a group of ladies to whom he was speaking that no one really realized how many mistakes the government had made. Shortly before this the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) suggested to the dairy

farmers in my riding that they should eat their own cheese; the price was too high to sell it abroad.
Also during the same campaign I had the pleasure of making the acquaintance of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). The great pleasure of this-and I say this sincerely- was marred only by the fact that, unfortunately, he mistook me for one of his supporters. However, as you may readily imagine, I immediately took appropriate steps to inform him that this was not the case at all.
The riding of Oxford, which I represent, is typical of many ridings in southwestern Ontario. It is half rural and half urban. The principal industry is dairy farming. But in this almost subtropical part of our country we also produce tobacco in considerable quantities. In the city of Woodstock and the towns of Tillsonburg and Ingersoll there are many very diversified manufacturing enterprises.
Because of the variety of ways in which my constituents make their living, naturally there are existing at present a variety of problems which are causing them considerable concern. Most of these particular problems have already been dealt with at some length and in great detail by various other hon. members during this debate; and accordingly, since I have no desire to be repetitious, I will touch on these matters only very briefly.
First of all I shall deal with the dairy industry. Broadly speaking, dairy farmers are very much concerned about the depressed price of cattle and dairy products generally. I should like to point out, however, that with regard to cheese, an enormous surplus of which had been built up due to lack of markets abroad-a condition about which the government seems to be able to do very little -the Ontario cheese producers' association, which is a producer board, succeeded recently by their own efforts in selling 10 million pounds abroad. This is the policy in agriculture which my party has been advocating for some time, namely that of producer boards who can make their own selling arrangements without interference from the government.
Also in regard to the dairy industry, there is at present a large stock of milk concentrates on hand. I am informed that today the amount is about 15 million pounds. It would seem to me that if the government is anxious to create good will in the countries of southeast Asia and parts of Europe, a very practical method of assistance would be to purchase and send large quantities of surplus stocks of milk concentrates to these countries. There is no finer or more nutritious form of food than milk, and this act would have the twofold purpose of creating good will abroad
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt while at the same time reducing the present stocks at home, which will eventually raise prices here.
I could not help noticing that, according to Saturday's issue of the London Free Press, the Prime Minister would appear to hold the same view. I find this item:
Prime Minister St. Laurent said today Canada is anxious to do anything possible for the relief or prevention of famine in other parts of the world.
I offer to the government this suggestion concerning milk concentrates available in the country.
Second, as to the tobacco industry, one of the chief concerns of tobacco growers at the present time is the government's continued policy of maintaining the high excise tax on cigarettes. As many hon. members may know, particularly those whose constituencies are close to the United States border, this has the disagreeable result of encouraging the smuggling of American cigarettes into this country on a scale that may not be realized even by the government. This, of course, has a tendency to reduce the number of Canadian cigarettes purchased and, accordingly, the amount of revenue flowing into the government coffers.
I would like to respectfully suggest that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), in compiling his next budget, consider reducing the excise tax on cigarettes to the extent that cigarettes can sell in this country for 25 cents for a package of 20.
Third, I would like to mention the subject of the textile industry. In the city of Woodstock alone, which has a population of approximately 17,000 persons, there are over 2,000 textile workers. Accordingly this subject is of the greatest interest to my constituents. The subject of the textile industry and its present problems has, of course, been presented to the government in great detail by the various textile unions and has already been presented in this house during this session by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. White) and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair). I would only like to add that I heartily endorse what both these hon. members have already said, and sincerely hope the government will take steps to tighten existing import regulations and will not make any treaty with Japan that will allow Japanese textiles, produced at incredibly low wages, to be brought into this country and destroy our textile industry.
There are in my constituency, however, one or two particular problems to which I hope the government may be persuaded to direct its attention. Oxford is a very beautiful county and a very delightful place in which to live, with many opportunities for-

The Address-Mr. Nesbitt people to pursue various lines of endeavour. For instance, if one were disposed to study archaeology one would indeed have to go no further than the Canadian National railway station in the city of Woodstock. This edifice, which was constructed shortly after the middle of the last century, is a delightful example of nineteenth century pioneer architecture, heated with a wood stove and quite unhampered by any twentieth century improvements. Despite the fact that one of the principal lines of the Canadian National Railways runs through Woodstock and does a very considerable business, the freight and passenger handling facilities are a disgrace. I would like to direct the request to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Ohevrier) that he please at least do something about this situation.
Like most of the rest of Canada, all southern Ontario was originally heavily forested, but because of the rich agricultural land in this part of the country these forests have long since been cleared away. As a result the land is no longer able to hold the moisture which falls in the largest quantity in the winter and spring; and accordingly in the spring the rivers in the area are raging torrents which erode and carry away the topsoil and in the past have flooded many of our cities, while in the summer these same streams dry up and almost disappear, causing severe problems of water supply for cattle and crops. Steps have already been taken to remedy this situation, and in my area the upper Thames valley authority has been established. This is a conservation project relating to the Thames river watershed. In this area various dams are proposed, and one indeed has been completed. The cost of these projects is divided between the federal government, the province and the municipalities, with the federal government and the province of Ontario paying the largest share.
The one dam already constructed in this large project is the Fanshawe dam near London, Ontario, and I had the pleasure of being present when it was opened early this fall by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and Premier Frost of Ontario. These dams, I might say, are intended to prevent spring floods which threaten the cities, towns and villages on the Thames river, and also to prevent the erosion of farm lands. The lakes created by these dams have a secondary purpose of creating supplies of water for the dry summer period and recreational facilities for the residents of this thickly populated area.
In this large plan it is proposed to construct two dams adjacent to the city of Woodstock, one on the Thames river immediately to the north of the city and one

on Cedar creek, a small tributary of the Thames to the south of the city. The construction of these dams will be greatly appreciated by many of my constituents, since my riding is not located adjacent to any of the great lakes and has no large bodies of water within its boundaries for recreational purposes, which, although secondary to the flood control and erosion purposes, are still very important to the ordinary citizen. I sincerely trust that the Minister of Public Works will direct his attention to the construction of these dams at an early date.
There are now two matters which are the general concern of all members of this house and of all citizens of the country. Both these matters have been dealt with at length by other hon. members during this debate, and I should merely like to add my voice to theirs on both these subjects, urging their adoption by the government. First is the subject of the removal of the means test for persons who are blind. Quite apart from any other consideration, I have found in my practice of law in the past that the means test often works a hardship on many of our very best citizens. Because of its arbitrary nature, many people with a sense of pride and self-reliance would rather do without pensions than subject themselves to an inquisition.
Often it seems that the less deserving members of our country are the ones who are successful in deriving these benefits. In this regard, since we believe in equality of opportunity in this country, it is my belief that all blind persons should receive pensions free of a means test. This pension in a small way merely helps equalize their opportunity to acquire the same income they could have earned if they were not without one of the most valuable physical assets which the rest of us possess.
Second, with regard to veterans allowances, I heartily endorse the recommendations made by other members of this house that veterans allowances be increased to $60 a month for single men and $120 a month for married men, and that the ceiling on permissive income, the total income these veterans may have, should be $1,200 a year in the case of single men and $2,000 a year in the case of married men.
It was with some regret that I noticed that the speech from the throne failed to be more specific on the subject of commonwealth relations. In the last half century the British commonwealth has afforded an example to the rest of the world on how various peoples with very diverse cultural, racial and economic backgrounds can arrive at their own self-determination by peaceful evolutionary

processes. I think hardly anyone in the world today would not agree that in this twentieth century of ours all countries of the world must learn to co-operate and if necessary sacrifice a degree of their national sovereignty in order that we may all survive and not be plunged into the holocaust of atomic war or worse.
During this century on two occasions an attempt has been made, at least, to form the beginnings of a world government. However, despite the high hopes of 1918 the first effort, the league of nations, came to grief for a multitude of reasons, the most important of which was probably national selfishness among the member nations.
After the second and more widespread world conflict of the last decade, another attempt has been made in this direction, the result of which remains largely to be seen, although I think most of us are at least hopeful as to what these results may be. In this connection, the most disturbing single factor in the world today is that while all countries on the planet give lip service to the need for international co-operation and many of these countries seem to be quite sincere, nevertheless since 1945 there has been a tremendous upswing of nationalism in many parts of the world, particularly in countries that have acquired their independence since the end of the recent war. Such nationalism is of course understandable, since many of these peoples in Asia and the Middle East now find themselves their own masters for the first time in centuries, in some cases.
Nationalism is a two-edged sword. If properly directed it can lead to a great expansion both in the cultural and economic productivity of a group of people with the accompanying benefits to all. On the other hand nationalism can also lead to war for the sole purpose of emphasizing, much like a small and not too reasonable boy, a people's self-assertiveness. These are the horns of the dilemma upon which the world rests today.
Again referring to the British commonwealth, it is the only organization of -an international type that has hung together in one form or another for the last hundred years. Now, however, we are unfortunately beginning to see signs of a break-up, and for no other reason than the misguided nationalism 'of each of the various individual units in the commonwealth. You will find very few people who do not think the idea of the commonwealth, with its co-operative discussion of problems amongst its member countries, is a good thing. On the other hand it seems apparent that the governments of 83276-31
The Address-Mr. Nesbitt many of the units of the commonwealth give lip service to this principle and at the same time, for reasons which can seem only related to local politics, deliberately encourage the wrong type of nationalism in their respective countries, which can only tend to break up the commonwealth. We have had some examples of this in this country but the more recent examples have been in Pakistan and Ceylon, where there is some discussion of becoming republics.
How to stop this unfortunate trend? One very humble suggestion which I would like to put forth, Mr. Speaker, is as follows. Why could not the various members of the commonwealth with dominion or republic status exchange governors general? For example, have Prime Minister Nehru of India as governor general of Canada some time in the future, and have Mr. Massey, for instance, go to Australia. I cannot help thinking this would not only set an excellent example for the rest of the world, but would also indicate to the people in the various countries of the commonwealth that they were all actually on an equal basis and that no one commonwealth country was in fact any more powerful or influential than another.
A further possible suggestion in this regard might be also that with modern transportation facilities Her Most Gracious Majesty might be persuaded to be present at the opening of the various commonwealth parliaments. This again could not help but act as a further unifying force within the commonwealth.
A number of my United States friends have often asked me to explain to them exactly what the relationship is between various commonwealth countries, as they admit they are rather at a loss to understand this arrangement. I have tried to explain it in the following way, which I think illustrates the point, and I hope the parallel will not find too much disfavour with the hon. members of the C.C.F. party.
Each country in the commonwealth is like a separate corporation; each with different shareholders and each with a totally different board of directors, and each manufacturing different varieties of products, sometimes in competition with one another and sometimes not. Each corporation, however, has the same honorary president, and it is the personal example set by this honorary president in relation to the various corporations that gives all the corporations a sense of relationship to one another. And it is this sense of relationship that often irons out and smooths over a great many problems and misunderstandings that might otherwise lead to serious trouble.

I sincerely hope the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) might take these very humble suggestions under consideration for possible future action.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I wish to make a few observations with respect to the need for experimental farms. However, may I first join in congratulating the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address which is the subject matter of this debate.
I should like to raise what I consider to be an important requirement in connection with farming in the three prairie provinces, and especially as it pertains to that part of Alberta from which I come. I refer now to the need in that and other areas in the west for additional experimental farms.
Let me deal first with Alberta. In that province we have oil, coal, natural gas, forests and other resources, but agriculture is still the basic industry and farming is the important occupation. The federal constituency which I have the honour to represent is typical in many respects of the province of Alberta. In my constituency you will find huge reserves of natural gas, and I expect that shortly there will be some discussion of this matter in this chamber. My constituency contains the Redwater oil field, one of the important centres in the oil industry in Canada. There is promise of new fields in my constituency as well as in other parts of the province. But, as I say, agriculture is still the basic industry and will continue to be.
Farming in western Canada is no longer a matter of the use of oxen and the walking plow, as it was with my grandfather over half a century ago, nor is it a matter of using horses. Farming in western Canada today is highly mechanized through the use of expensive machinery. The labour saving as a result of the use of this machinery probably explains the loss of population in the rural areas.
There is one thing with which western Canada is confronted at all times, the cost of production. We depend on export markets. Because of our distance from markets and because of the high cost of transportation, production cost is a most important factor if the farmer is to survive in his occupation. Furthermore, farming today must be carried on on a scientific and businesslike basis. Many problems have arisen in recent years such as soil erosion, the control of noxious weeds, the best methods of soil control to be used, and many others.


This is where the experimental farm plays such an important role. It provides expert advice to the farmer and is a source of firsthand information in the respective communities. I feel that the experimental farms we have in western Canada have been of great service to agriculture. But there is one suggestion I should like to make. Although these experimental farms have done great service, because of their distance one from another they do not provide an opportunity to many farmers to make use of them.
One example I could give is provided by my own constituency. The nearest dominion experimental farm to Vegreville constituency is at Lacombe. In the case of many farmers this represents a distance of 200 miles or more. Yet Vegreville constituency is one of the most thickly populated rural areas in western Canada. This constituency has produced many oats and barley winners at the Toronto royal winter fair and the Chicago world show. Only a few days ago Charles J. Kallal and William Melnyk, farmers in my constituency, won top honours for their cattle.
It is my submission to the government, and particularly to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), that instead of increasing the size of experimental farms like the one at Lacombe we should have something on probably a smaller scale scattered throughout the west, and especially in such areas as northeastern Alberta. A chance should be given to such establishments to build themselves up. I am not thinking merely of demonstration farms; I am thinking of something bigger than that.
It would then be convenient for farmers to visit the experimental farms to get firsthand information on the various experiments being conducted and see how they can improve their farming operations, increase their production and above all cut down their cost of production.
There is another matter I want to deal with at this time, and that is the statements made in this house by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) in his defence of United States Senator McCarthy. I do not think we in this house need concern ourselves too much with United States personalities except in so far as they affect us in this country, and I do not think I need to defend the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), because he is well able to take care of himself.
When the hon. member for Spadina made reference to McCarthyism and McCarthyites, I felt he made that reference at a time when it was necessary, a time when the hand of McCarthyism was stretching across into

Canada, a time when there were slurring insinuations of communist sympathies made against the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
The hon. member for Lethbridge has asked what is meant by McCarthyism and what is meant by McCarthyites, and I shall endeavour to answer that question by citing a recent example which occurred in this house. I must add that I do so with some reluctance, but I feel it necessary to do so because there is and has been a great deal of feeling among my constituents, and I was specifically instructed to raise this question during this session of the House of Commons.
I am referring, of course, as hon. members will remember, to the period when I first came into this house, in 1949, when a member of the Social Credit party, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) took it upon himself to condemn the people in my constituency and make slurring remarks and insinuations. He insinuated that in Vegre-ville there was nothing but a lot of communists, and added that I had been elected by the communist vote, and that although communism had failed throughout Canada Vegreville was the one place it had succeeded. That was at the time of my election. That was the accusation that was made in this house in 1949.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind some of the members in that Social Credit group that since that time there has been another election, namely on August 10 last. At that time we had about 100 communist candidates throughout Canada,- including a communist in the Vegreville federal constituency. Throughout Canada every communist candidate lost his deposit, including the communist candidate in Vegreville. Another thing that is somewhat significant is that this same Social Credit candidate who tried to be elected again was not elected, in spite of the fact that he spent the past four years conducting a personal house to house campaign.
I mention this, Mr. Speaker, because when we listen to McCarthyism, when we listen to the hon. member defending Senator McCarthy, and when I think of this Social Credit group I am reminded of Edgar Bergen. Most of us I think have heard Edgar Bergen on the radio. He is another United States personality, and I think Senator McCarthy is like Edgar Bergen. He has in Canada's House of Commons little McCarthys or Charlie Mc-Carthys with, Mr. Speaker, a Mortimer Snerd for good measure.
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like most of the members who sit on the opposition benches I am more disappointed at what the speech from the throne does not contain than I am about what it does contain. I was very disappointed to find no mention made in the speech from the throne of any intention on the part of the government to improve old age pensions during this session. I want to remind ministers on the government side that while we talk about undernourished and underfed people in Asian countries we have in this country our own older citizens by the thousands who have to live on a paltry $40 a month pension and who, when they have paid their rent and their bills at the drug stores, have very little left to live on and are actually going hungry in this prosperous country of ours.
I am disappointed that there is no mention in the speech from the throne of any intention on the part of the government to remove the means test from the veterans allowance, or to remove the means test for the blind, and no intention of liberalizing unemployment insurance regulations. I would suggest to the cabinet that the time has come when unless unemployment insurance regulations are liberalized there will arise in this country a demand for their liberalization of such a nature that it will probably wreck our unemployment insurance program. The time-is overripe for some liberalization of these unemployment insurance regulations.
I am disappointed in the proposed housing' legislation. Last spring I introduced in this house a C.C.F. program for housing. We recommended, among other things, an extension of the amortization period and a reduction in the down payment. In so far as the proposed legislation will extend that amortization period and reduce the down payment I think it is good. However, we couple these reforms with the condition that the government itself should lend government money at 2 per cent for the building of low rental housing. I am confident that the proposed legislation, while it may tinker with the N.H.A., will not by any manner of means remedy our housing situation or meet the needs of those in our community who cannot provide homes for themselves at present-day costs.
I am sorry to find there is no mention in the speech from the throne of provision for houses for veterans. I have found that the people in this country who are suffering most from our housing conditions are the returned veterans with large families. I have in mind the case of a veteran with six small children. The house in which that veteran is living has been sold and he has received an eviction

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy notice. I personally applied on his behalf to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I applied to the veterans affairs people in Toronto; I applied to our municipal and metropolitan housing authorities. The only suggestion offered was that made by veterans affairs, and their suggestion was that the man concerned should pull up stakes in Toronto, take his family and move north some place where he could get a job and a house in which to live.
I suggest that is not good enough, Mr. Speaker, for a man who served five years in this country's service overseas. The veterans affairs people tell me that a few years ago, before the government undertook to sell their government-owned houses, they were in a position to meet such a condition as that. But the government has been so eager to get out of the housing business and to dispose of the houses they owned during the war that today the veterans affairs people have just no place to which they can recommend a veteran, no matter how dire the circumstances may be in which he finds himself.
I want to spend most of my time, Mr. Speaker, dealing with another subject that is mentioned in the throne speech; I refer to the reference to a proposed extension of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. I feel that I have some qualification to speak on gold mining in that, at one time and another, I have worked in the gold mines at every process in mining and milling from mucking to refining. I know from firsthand experience the hazardous nature of that occupation, as well as the arduous nature of it.
Before this house opened I spent a week with the men who are now on strike in northern Ontario and Quebec. I talked with them and their families. I talked with the businessmen in the communities that are now affected by that strike. Again from firsthand experience I know of the suffering which these men, their families and their communities are undergoing during the present strike in that area.
I want to deal with this matter now instead of waiting until the legislation is brought down because from experience I have learned that it is much easier to get the ear of the government and get them to consider a measure before it is brought down in the house than after it has been brought down. I am quite confident that if the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mrs. Shipley) and the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Eyre) were sitting on opposition benches instead of on government benches they would long ago have


spoken in the interests of the gold miners and the communities now suffering from the strike.
Just recently there came to my desk, and I presume it came to the desks of other hon. members, a portfolio of material setting forth the case for the mine owners as against that of the miners. The portfolio consisted of material from the report handed down by the chairman of one board of conciliation, the last of seven that sat on these cases. The chairman of that one board-one out of seven that have dealt with this problem-expressed some doubt about granting the voluntary revocable check-off to the miners because of an outbreak of violence which had occurred early in the strike. I may simply add that the miners' point of view was not sent to us, nor the comment made by the miners' representative on that board of conciliation. We received one side of the story only.
The case for the mine owners has been well taken care of in the financial pages of some of our papers. I want to set forth to the best of my ability the case for the miners themselves. Some days ago I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) whether, in view of the federal government's interest in gold mining, his department had taken any action to assist in bringing about a settlement of that strike. As reported at page 81 of Hansard the minister's reply was as follows:
. . . the gold mining industry comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, and since I have had no communication from the provincial government in this connection, my department has taken no action in the matter.
The question that immediately arose in my mind when I heard that answer was this. Was the federal government as much concerned with provincial rights in the matter of gold mines when the question of subsidizing these mines came up for consideration in 1948, and when amendments to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act were brought down in later years? Did the provincial governments concerned appeal to the federal government for assistance to the gold mines? To me it is quite evident that the provincial governments or the federal government, or both, were much more concerned about subsidizing the profits of the mine owners than they were about assisting the miners and the communities which are affected by this strike. Did the federal government proceed to subsidize gold mining with complete disregard for provincial rights in gold mining, or did the provincial governments apply for that aid? In either case, one or the other or both evidenced much more

interest in subsidizing the mine owners' profits than they did in the welfare of the people concerned.
I trust the Minister of Labour will clarify that point for us. When he is doing that, there are at least two other points on which I should like to have some clarification. Have any steps been taken by the federal government to make sure that Canadian taxpayers' money is not being used to offset the cost of the strike, or a part of the cost of the strike, to the mine owners? In regulation 17 I notice that where a mine is closed down for a period of 30 days or more, such help may be given. It is apparently left to the discretion of the minister to decide whether or not such assistance shall be given.
In the government's report on the administration of the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act I also notice that in 1951, when the Hollinger mine was on strike for nine weeks, the amount of cost aid per ounce was well over $1 more than it was in 1950 when the mine was not on strike, and was more than it was in 1952 when there was no strike. I am simply asking the minister what steps the government took in 1951 to see that the taxpayers' money was not used to subsidize, in part at least, the costs of the strike to the mine owners.
I heard only today that another mine, the Paymaster mine, will close down on December 17 when its present contract with the miners expires. This mine will be closed for less than 30 days in 1953. According to my reading of the regulations there is no question in the world but that this mine, being closed down for less than 30 days, can apply this government cost aid subsidy to offset part of the cost to the mine of this period when it is shut down.
I say to the government, the government that is so careful to avoid the issue of provincial rights so far as a strike is concerned, that if they are permitting any part of the cost aid subsidy to offset the cost of a strike to the mine operators, then they are not maintaining a neutral position in this strike, a position which they profess to be maintaining. I would point out further that in the case of the Unemployment Insurance Act, it specifically states that no employee shall receive unemployment insurance while he is on strike. I submit that on the same basis no mine owner should receive federal assistance to help him cover the cost of a strike when such strike is in progress.
I note from page 8 of the report of the administration of emergency gold mining assistance that production costs include almost everything imaginable in connection with
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy mining and milling, together with the cost of exploration and development. Then on page 9 we are told that the allowable exploration and development costs incurred each week are verified by an inspecting engineer during a yearly field inspection trip. I ask the minister, is he confident that one annual visit of an inspecting engineer is sufficient to assure the government that the mine owners are not taking advantage of this subsidy to charge up development and exploration costs to a greater extent than is permitted under the regulations?
What knowledge has the government, for instance, of the amount of backfill the Hollinger mine has piled up for use in future years since it has been receiving cost aid from the federal government? What steps has the federal government taken to ensure that the piling up of that backfill is in accordance with the regulations laid down under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act? What precautions are taken by the government to ensure that these mines are not deliberately keeping their mill heads low in order to mill their low-grade ore while the government subsidy is available, and sealing off their higher grade ore until such time as they can get a higher price for gold or a higher subsidy from this government? I have met miners in northern Ontario who told me their job has been to seal off high-grade ore whenever it was discovered and to keep it for future development, while the low-grade ore was fed to the mill and emergency gold mining assistance used in order to pay for part of the cost of that milling.
Those are some questions that I suggest the minister take into consideration before introducing legislation which will extend the emergency gold mining assistance for another year. I am not suggesting for a moment that I am opposed to this emergency gold mining assistance. I am merely pointing out that if the government finds it necessary to subsidize the gold mines, then some measure must be taken to see that this benefit from the public treasury goes to the miners and the community, and is not all siphoned off in profits for shareholders and speculative stock buyers.
I want to deal with a few points in connection with this strike in more detail. In the first place I want to say that, in my opinion, the present strike in the gold mines in northern Ontario and Quebec was deliberately provoked by the mine owners with a view to forcing either a higher price for gold or a higher subsidy from this government. To this point at least there is not the slightest bit of evidence that these mine owners made any effort whatever to avert the strike. I

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy refer to the mine owners because I think if the management of some of these mines were free from absentee ownership the situation would have been different. In the first six of the majority reports submitted by boards of conciliation the findings were in favour of the miners' requests. These six reports advised an increase in wages, a reduction in the 48-hour week, and the adoption of the voluntary revocable check-off. Only in one of these seven reports was there a finding adverse to the miners. This report was made on the basis of outbreaks of violence which had occurred.
While speaking on that subject, may I remind hon. members of a statement made last week by the chief of police of Timmins on one of our national broadcasts. He stated that there had been a reduction in crime in the mining camps by 50 per cent since the strike began, and attributed that reduction to the co-operation which he had received from the miners' union itself.
Here are some of the men. I want the house to know the calibre of the men who have made these recommendations. There is Mr. Eric Taylor, prominent businessman and industrialist, a mediator with a record of settlements in industrial disputes that is probably the best in Ontario. He is a former vice-president of Brazilian Traction company, and a labour relations specialist for Canadian Industries Limited. He is also on the staff of the University of Montreal, and by no stretch of the imagination can he be considered to be partial in favour of the miners. Mr. Taylor made recommendations which the miners, through their unions, offered to accept, and are still ready to accept if the mine managers or owners will consider them.
Then His Honour Judge Wilfred S. Lane of Picton, Ontario, served as chairman of a number of successful boards of conciliation, including the dispute between the running trades and the railways. His recommendations, made two years ago, have yet to be implemented by the McIntyre mine. The union was and still is ready to accept the recommendations of Judge Lane, but the mine owners have rebuffed every one of those recommendations.
His Honour Judge Harold E. Fuller of Welland, Ontario, has handled some of the toughest labour relations and conciliation problems in Ontario. He has won settlements involving such giant corporations as Algoma Steel, International Harvester Company, and others. Three years ago he submitted recommendations which, had the mine owners been willing to accept them, not only would have averted this strike but would

have established friendly labour relations between labour and management in that camp.
Professor C. H. Curtis, specialist in labour relations and professor in labour management at Queen's University, Kingston, made inquiries this year from which he was able to conclude that the companies could increase wages and lower hours, in spite of the price of gold. The miners through their unions were and still are ready to accept the recommendations of Professor Curtis.
Again, it is the mine owners who have refused to compromise on a single one of these recommendations. There is not a single shred of evidence that these operators have made any attempt to avert a strike. Had the operators been willing even to try to reach an agreement the strike, which is now crippling a community of 50,000 people, would have been averted.
Gold mining is about the only industry in this country where the employees, through their union, in many instances are given no opportunity to negotiate wage agreements or agreements as to hours, conditions of work, welfare and other matters of interest to the workers. Gold mining operators, especially the operators of the larger mines, have been interested in one phase of mining only; that is mining for profit for the shareholders and the mining stock speculators. They assume they have some God-given right to the ownership of our natural resources, and some God-given right to exploit those natural resources without regard for the welfare of the workers or the welfare of the community. They have sought through the years to evade municipal responsibilities and municipal taxation. They have sought tax concessions from provincial and federal governments alike. While on the one hand they have very astutely invested their profits for the benefit of shareholders, they have invested nothing for the broken-down bodies of the miners who have worn themselves out digging gold. With the support of a portion of our press they have succeeded in selling to the public the idea that gold mining is a depressed industry, that the capital invested is risk capital, and that consequently it is entitled to more than normal profits.
Just to what extent is capital invested in gold mining today risk capital, and therefore entitled to a higher rate of profit than is received in other industries? In the first place, the price of gold is not fixed at $35 an ounce. It is not even subject to the old law of supply and demand. The mines have an option of selling a portion of their gold on the open market or selling it to the federal government, and they may choose whichever

is the more profitable. But the gold that is sold to the Canadian government is not sold for $35 an ounce.
The price of gold to the Canadian government depends upon the cost of production. The higher the cost of production, the more cost aid the mine receives and the more the mine owner gets for his gold. It is conceivable, though I do not think it has happened as yet, that a mine could receive maximum cost aid, which for 1953 is $13.50 per ounce, so their gold would be sold for an equivalent of 35 United States dollars, plus $13.50-that is, not for $35 but rather for $48.50 per ounce. In fact, in the case of one mine in 1952 the cost aid ran to $14.50 per ounce, making the price of gold for that operator not $35 but $49.50 per ounce.
Then, much of the risk of gold mining has been taken over not only by our cost aid program but by the services and facilities made available to the mines both by provincial and federal governments. The federal and provincial governments alike maintain mining branches for the express purpose of assisting mines, gold mines included, in exploration, mapping and improving the various processes which enter into mining and milling. If gold mining is a depressed industry, it is the wages of the miners that are depressed and not the profits of the mine owners. According to table C6 in the Labour Gazette for October, 1953, the average weekly wage for gold mining was $60.04. That average wage, by the way, includes the highly publicized bonus which miners receive. The gold mining average was $60.04. The average weekly wage for other metal mining was $69.10. Gold miners were receiving $9.06 a week less than miners in other fields. There has been no increase in wages in gold mining in Ontario and Quebec since 1951.
Amendments were made to the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act in 1952 which increased the amount of cost aid which a mine could receive. None of that cost aid was passed on to the miners. The operators, without a single exception, rejected the recommendations of boards of conciliation for an increase of 7 to 10 cents an hour, and are still insisting that miners work through 1954 for the same wages they received in 1951, in spite of the increased cost of living and in spite of the fact that our 1953 cost aid will put at least $3 million more in the coffers and the profits of the gold mining shareholders.
Are we as custodians of the taxpayers' interests to stand idly by, or to sit idly by, while gold mine operators pass on all the cost aid they can possibly extract from this government to profits, with cold-blooded,

Mr. Noseworthy calculated indifference alike to miners and mining communities? I suggest that the basis on which cost aid is given be reviewed in order to make certain that miners as well as mine owners benefit from these federal subsidies.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a couple of minutes to deal with profits in gold mining. I have said that profits in gold mining are not depressed. They are not depressed if compared with profits made by investors in other industries. One of the mines now on strike, one of those which received cost aid in 1952, showed a net profit in that year equal to 28 per cent of their net worth. Their net profit in 1952, after all imaginable write-offs and taxes, comes within a few thousand dollars of their total paid-up capital. That is one of the mines now on strike, one of the mines which was receiving cost aid, and one which pretends that it cannot afford to increase wages. The McIntyre mine-

Just because these mines have been making fabulous profits over the years is no reason why they are still entitled to profits on a similar scale at the expense of Canadian taxpayers, the miners and the mining communities.
I see that my time has expired. I merely want to appeal again to the minister responsible for this act to take some steps to see that if mine owners are to benefit by this cost aid program, the miners themselves and the communities concerned also derive some benefit from the program.
